# The Hunter's Moon

I shouldn't have come out here.

The forest was a cathedral of black pine, the moon a sick coin pressed against the clouds, and somewhere behind me a branch cracked—not the snap of an animal fleeing, but the slow, deliberate *crack* of something testing its weight against rotten wood.

I stopped breathing. My hands curled around the straps of my camera.

*Move,* something whispered. *Run.*

But my legs had become stones.

Another sound. A wet, tearing pop, like someone pulling a wishbone apart in a stew pot. Then a low, gurgling keen that didn't belong to anything with a throat I'd ever seen.

*It's hurt. Some animal caught in a trap. Walk toward the sound. Help it.*

I was twenty feet away when I saw the man.

He was on his knees in a clearing, his shirt half-removed, his body bent forward as if praying to a god I didn't recognize. I could see the sheen of sweat across his shoulders, the dark mat of hair on his back, the slow rise and fall of breath.

"Sir?" My voice came out as a mousetrap. "Are you—"

He turned his head.

The face that looked back at me was *wrong* in a way my brain kept trying to unsee. The jaw had dropped. Not unhinged—*lengthened*, the chin pulling forward as if it were made of clay, the skin beneath it stretching like taffy pulled between two fists. I watched a tendon slide beneath the surface of his cheek, watched his mouth extend into something almost canine, the lips peeling back to reveal teeth that were—*oh God*—*growing*—

He screamed. Or tried to. The sound came out as a gurgling howl, half-human, half-something that remembered wolves.

I dropped my camera.

His spine *arched*. I heard it before I saw it—a sound like a baseball bat striking a pumpkin, the wet crunch of vertebrae separating, one from another, pushing outward. The skin of his back split in three long red seams, and through them I saw something white and glistening push and *grow*—the knobs of his spine, dragging new bone into places bone had no business being. His shoulders hunched, hunched again, then *rolled* forward with a pop that made me taste copper at the back of my tongue.

His arms were next. I watched the fingers curl, uncurl, then the *knuckles* popped outward, each one like a small-caliber gunshot, and the hands themselves elongated, the nails blackening, curling, lengthening into something I had seen only on the snares of trappers' photographs. The skin of his forearms split along invisible seams, dark wet fur pushing through like a field of black grass growing in time-lapse.

The smell hit me then. Iron and hot fur and something sweeter, like the inside of a warm animal.

He rose onto all fours. The motion was *wrong*—too fluid, as if his joints had been re-engineered. His thighs split the seams of his trousers, the muscles bunching and rolling under skin that was no longer human skin but a dark pelt, coarse and bristling. His head swung up toward the moon, and I saw the last of the man's face collapse into something lupine—the forehead sloping back, the ears crawling up his skull and pointing, the muzzle lengthening until the eyes were almost lost behind the bridge of the new nose.

The bones of his face *crunched* inward, reshaping, the eye sockets squeezing, the jaw hinging open to let out a sound—

The howl came down out of his throat like something being born in agony, and every hair on my body stood on end.

The thing that had been a man turned its yellow eyes on me.

They were the worst part. The eyes were still *his*.

I ran.

# The Victorian Operating Theatre

The scene unfolds in a wood-panelled amphitheatre at a London teaching hospital, perhaps in the 1850s. Tiered benches rise around a central wooden table stained dark with the residue of countless previous operations. The surgeon enters to the expectant hush of medical students who have paid for the privilege of observation.

## The Preparation

The patient, a labourer whose limb has been crushed beyond repair by industrial machinery, is held down by burly assistants. Often a leather strap or a leather bite-gag is offered — sometimes the patient refuses, preferring to scream. Whiskey or opium may have been administered, but the effect is minimal against what's coming. The surgeon pulls on a frock coat — not a clean gown, but a garment stiffened with the dried blood of dozens of prior patients, considered a mark of experience rather than a hygiene concern.

The instruments gleam coldly: a curved amputation knife, a saw with a sharp blade, catgut ligatures, bone wax.

## The Speed

Speed was not a luxury but a necessity. The patient was conscious, and the surgeon's reputation depended on performing the procedure before the patient could physically react. Robert Liston, the era's most famous "fastest knife in the West End," was renowned for a leg amputation reportedly completed in under 30 seconds. A student holding a stopwatch timed him.

**"Time me, gentlemen!"** the surgeon might call out, as he does in this reconstruction. The famous Liston quote: *"Time me, gentlemen, time me!"*

## The Incision

A single sweeping circular cut through skin, muscle, and fascia — the surgeon's arm moving in one continuous arc. The assistant's fingers compress the main artery against the bone. Then the surgeon takes the saw and works rapidly through the bone, the sound filling the theatre. Finally, the severed limb drops, sometimes into a sawdust box beneath the table.

## The Blood and the Sound

Blood flows freely. There is no notion of sterile technique — germ theory is not yet accepted. The assistant presses a red-hot iron or chemical cautery to the severed vessels, the hissing and smoke filling the room. Ligatures are tied. The stump is closed, often left to heal by secondary intention.

And the patient — the patient has screamed. Not a single cry, but a sustained, animal sound that echoes off the wooden walls. Some patients reportedly went into shock and remembered nothing. Others, tragically, remembered everything. Soldiers at Waterloo and the Crimean War described the amputation tent as the worst horror of battlefield medicine — worse than the wound itself.

---

This grim reality is precisely what drove the desperate search for anesthesia. When William Morton's 1846 demonstration of ether reached Britain, surgeons like Liston himself became enthusiastic adopters within weeks — not out of sudden humanitarianism, but because the new technique was simply a gift to their craft. A few breaths of ether, and the screaming stopped. The age of the spectator sport of surgery, where students timed the butcher-surgeons, finally drew to a close.

# The Choice

The rain hadn't stopped in three days, and it drummed against the corrugated roof of the old gas station like a thousand impatient fingers. Maya sat with her back against the wall, Lena's head resting in her lap, smoothing the wet hair from her forehead the way she'd done when Lena was a child and had come down with the flu.

That was twelve years ago. A different world.

"He's going to ask you to do it," Lena whispered. Her voice was thin, stretched to gossamer. "I know how his mind works."

"I know."

"I don't want him to carry it. That's why I'm telling you."

Maya didn't answer. Outside, a door creaked. The patrol was back. She heard Carlos's boots first, heavy and deliberate, then the lighter steps of Tom. And finally the careful, measured footsteps of David, who always walked like a man trying not to disturb something sleeping.

They came around the corner in the dim light of a single battery lantern. David stopped when he saw them. His face did a thing Maya had learned to read over the years—a series of small collapses, each one hidden behind the next.

"The perimeter's secure," Carlos said, but his voice trailed off when he saw Lena. He set his rifle against the wall and sat down heavily.

Tom remained standing. He couldn't look at Lena, which meant he already knew.

"How long?" David asked.

Lena answered. "I can feel it in my blood, David. Hours. Maybe less. I watched my mother go through this. I know what comes next."

David lowered himself to the floor across from them. The lantern threw their shadows long against the wall behind—four figures, one of which had begun to blur at the edges.

"David." Lena's hand reached for him, and he took it, and Maya saw the way his grip tightened, the way his jaw set like he was trying to hold his whole life together with his teeth. Twenty-three years they had been together. Twenty-three years of small arguments over coffee, of forehead kisses in the dark, of the quiet kind of love that doesn't need to announce itself.

"Tell me you can get the medicine," Lena said to him. "Tell me you have it somewhere."

"I don't."

"Then we stop pretending."

The silence that followed had a weight to it. A physical thing pressing on all of them. Carlos pulled a rag from his pocket and twisted it between his hands, the way a man used to fold napkins at a restaurant a long time ago.

"Tom, sit down," Maya said softly. Tom sat, but on the edge of the circle, like he was still trying to keep one foot in the exit.

"She was bit six hours ago," David said, as if he were reading from some report. "The site is on her left shoulder. She said it was a child. A little girl. It came out of the dark so fast she didn't have time to—"

"I know what happened," Lena said. "I was there."

Carlos finally spoke. "I had a brother. In Texas. Danny. He was bit on a supply run, and I—I was the one who—"

He didn't finish. He didn't need to.

"Everybody here has done it," Tom said, and his voice cracked on the last word. "That's why we make the rule. That's why we say what we say about it. Because the alternative is—" He gestured vaguely toward the darkness outside, where things moved in the wet woods that had once been suburbs, that had once been schools, that had once been everything.

"The alternative is watching her turn into one of them," Lena said. "The alternative is sending David out to do it when she's still trying to tear his face off. Don't you see? This is the only kindness left."

Maya felt Lena's hand find hers. The skin was already cooling. The clock was already running.

"I'll do it," Maya said.

"Maya—" David began.

"I'll do it because she asked. And because you have to keep going after this. All of you. And I can do this one thing, and then I can walk away from you, and you don't have to look at me every day and remember."

She didn't say the other part. That she had been the one to hold Lena when her mother died. That she had been the one to teach Lena how to shoot. That she had been the one to carry Lena over a river when her foot was broken, even though they both nearly drowned, even though they laughed about it afterward in a way they never laughed about anything else.

You don't get to be the kind of friends they'd been and pretend this would be nothing.

"I love you," Lena said to all of them. "I love you and I'm not afraid and I need you to believe that, because if you think I'm afraid, you won't be able to do it, and then I'll come back as something that isn't me, and I'll kill you, and that'll be the last thing I do in this world."

David made a sound. It wasn't a word. It was the sound a man makes when his chest cracks open but he has to keep breathing anyway.

Maya bent down and pressed her lips to Lena's forehead. "I love you too, you stubborn woman."

"I know."

She looked up at David, and he looked at her, and something passed between them that didn't need language—a permission, a forgiveness, a promise that the rest of their lives would not be easy but that they would not be alone in them.

Maya stood. She walked to the corner where the medical supplies were kept, and she picked up the bottle, and she measured the dose, and she filled the syringe, and she did it all with the careful precision of a person performing the only sacrament their world had left.

When she came back, Lena's eyes were closed. Her breathing was slowing. But when Maya knelt beside her, she opened them, and they were still *her*—still brown and sharp and full of that particular Lena light that had been the first thing to make Maya laugh after the world ended.

"I'm going to give you something," Maya said. "You're going to feel sleepy, and then you're going to be warm, and then you're going to be done."

"Okay."

"David, you should—"

"No. I'm staying. I'm staying with her."

Lena smiled. It was a terrible smile, because it was real, because it was happening, because in a moment it would be a memory instead of a face.

"You boys get out," she said, to Carlos and Tom. "Go check the east fence. You know it needs mending."

Tom stood, hesitated, and then left. Carlos followed, but he paused at the corner and looked back, and his eyes were wet, and he nodded once, just once, at Maya, and then he was gone.

The rain was louder now. The lantern flickered. Somewhere in the woods, a branch cracked, and none of them cared.

"I'm ready," Lena said.

Maya found the vein. She looked at David. He nodded, the smallest motion, the kind of motion a man makes when the world has just ended for the second time in his life.

Lena sighed. "Tell me about the cabin. The one we were going to find."

"The one with the blue shutters," Maya said.

"Blue shutters. And the apple tree. And the porch swing you were going to hang."

"That's right. We were going to sit on it every evening and not do anything. Just sit."

"Just sit." Lena's eyes were closing. "I would have liked that."

Her breathing slowed. It shallowed. It became something almost imperceptible, a thread of a thing, a memory of a breath.

"I love you," Maya whispered.

"I know," Lena said, or maybe didn't say, or maybe only thought, and then she was gone, and the space she left behind was enormous, and the rain kept falling, and the world kept turning, and Maya sat there for a long time, holding the hand of someone she had known for seventeen years and would now know for the rest of her life.

Outside, the morning was beginning, gray and wet and indifferent.

There was still fence to mend.

# The Corner

---

It started with David, of all people.

Not the murder itself, though that was a thing that had happened, a thing tucked now behind a door in his mind that he kept meaning to lock more securely. The murder had been necessary, in the way that David himself had once called necessary things *necessary*, with that particular tilt of his head. Marcus could still hear it. That was the problem.

It was three weeks after. Marcus was washing dishes. The kitchen window was dark, and his own reflection hung there, watery and distorted, and just to the right of his own shoulder —

He turned.

Nothing. The counter. A mug. A sponge going gray with old coffee.

He laughed, softly, at himself. Went to bed. Slept poorly.

---

By the second month, he had learned not to turn.

That was the first real lesson the madness taught him: *don't look directly at it.* If you look, it scatters. If you look, you admit you've seen it. And if you admit you've seen it, then you are the kind of person who sees such things, and you must either be mad or guilty, and the two are not the same but they live in the same neighborhood, and the rents are bad.

So he trained himself. He trained the way a horse is trained, through the patient application of not-yet. *Not yet don't look. Not yet don't turn. Not yet don't acknowledge.*

David stood in the hallway when Marcus came home from work. Just standing. Hands at his sides. The way David had stood in the doorway the night of the party, watching Marcus across the room with a small, knowing smile, before he'd opened his mouth and —

Marcus set his keys down carefully. Hung his coat. Stepped past the figure in the hallway without turning his head. He could feel it the way you feel a cold window in a warm room: a presence of *not*, a place where the air was doing something other than air.

He made dinner. He ate at the table. He did not look at the empty chair across from him, because the empty chair was not the problem. The problem was the figure standing behind it, half in shadow, patient as a lamp.

---

This is how the rot works, and I am telling you this so you understand it is not sudden. It is a *furnishings* thing, the way a house goes bad. The leak starts in a place you cannot see, in a pipe behind a wall, and by the time the wallpaper begins to stain, the joists are already weeping, already soft.

First, the small accommodations. You begin to plan your movements around the figure. You learn which rooms it favors. You learn its hours. You begin to set a place at meals out of habit, and then out of superstition, and then out of a kind of weary domesticity, the way a prisoner learns to love the shape of his cell because love is easier than the alternative.

Marcus began to talk to it.

He told himself he wasn't. He told himself he was talking to the empty room, the same way people talk to empty rooms, which everyone does, which is normal, which is a thing normal people do. He said, *I had a long day.* He said, *The neighbors are being loud again.* He said, *I don't know what to do about the leak in the bathroom.*

The figure did not answer. The figure never answered. That was, in its way, the worst of it, because David had always answered. David had never, in life, not answered. He had been a man made of opinions and interjections, a man who had filled every silence the way weather fills a valley. And now the silence was the answer, and the silence was everywhere, and the silence had the shape of David in it, standing just past the edge of seeing, holding still.

---

By the fifth month, Marcus was sleeping with the lights on.

This is not the madness, though. This is only the symptom. The madness is something else, something quieter, something that has been happening in the basement of him for weeks while he was busy watching the figure in the corner of his eye.

The madness is this: he begins to *like* it.

Not the guilt. The guilt is a separate animal, and it lives in his chest, and it eats. The madness is the other thing, the thing that grows in the soil the guilt has fertilized. The madness is the slow, horrible realization that the figure has begun to feel like *company.* That the apartment without it is worse than the apartment with it. That the long quiet evenings, which used to be the punishment, are now the *reward*, because this is when David comes, and stands, and does not leave.

Marcus is appalled by this. He catalogs the ways in which he is appalled, which is its own kind of madness, the self-surveillance of the damned. He watches himself watching the figure. He notices when he begins to *arrange* things for it. He buys a second mug. He leaves a light on in the hallway. He finds himself, one evening, standing in the doorway of the kitchen the way David used to stand, with that small tilt of the head, and he catches his own reflection in the dark window and does not recognize which one of them is looking back.

---

Here is the part that no one tells you about going mad, which is that it is mostly *waiting.*

You wait for the figure to move. You wait for it to speak. You wait, in the small hours, for the moment when the eye slides toward the corner and the figure is closer than it was yesterday, or further, or changed in some way you cannot name but which you have memorized. You wait, and you do the dishes, and you go to work, and you come home, and the figure is there, and the waiting is over, and then begins again.

Marcus had thought, in the first days, that he was being punished. This is the natural thought. This is the thought of a man who still believes in a moral universe, who believes that the world keeps accounts, who believes that if he has done a thing then the thing will be done back to him, neatly, as a mirror does it.

But the figure is not a punishment. A punishment would end. A punishment would have a sentence, a release, a moment when the cell opens and the air outside smells different. The figure does not end. The figure is not a sentence. The figure is a *climate.*

Marcus is the climate. Marcus is the weather now. The guilt and the figure and the long slow rot of him have become a system, an ecosystem, a small closed world with its own laws, and he is the only animal in it, and he is both the predator and the prey, and the figure in the corner of his eye is neither, and is both, and is the only other thing alive.

---

On the night he finally looks directly at it, it is raining.

He doesn't plan it. He has spent six months not planning it, has built his whole life around the architecture of *not*, has become a man whose whole existence is a careful sideways sentence, a man who only ever looks at things from the corner, who only ever speaks to the room, who only ever acknowledges the world in the peripheral grammar of the unsaid.

But the rain is loud, and the apartment is small, and David is standing in the hallway again, and something in Marcus — some joist that has been weeping for months, some beam finally giving way — just *turns.*

He turns his whole head. He looks.

David is there.

He is exactly as he was. He is not translucent, which is the thing that surprises Marcus, the thing that the stories never got right. He is not a mist. He is not a suggestion. He is a man, standing in a hallway, in a perfectly ordinary apartment, on a perfectly ordinary night, and he looks at Marcus, and Marcus looks at him, and the rain is loud, and the light from the kitchen falls on David's face the way light has always fallen on faces, which is to say *fully*, which is to say *without mercy.*

David opens his mouth.

And the terrible thing, the thing that breaks the last of the beams, the thing that lets the ceiling finally come down — the terrible thing is that Marcus cannot tell, even now, whether David is about to speak or whether David has just spoken or whether David has been speaking, for six months, in a language Marcus has spent six months learning to almost-hear.

He will never know.

He will spend the rest of his life in the hallway. He will spend the rest of his life in the small warm climate of the rot. The figure will be there, and he will look at it, and the rain will be loud, and the light will fall, and somewhere in the walls the pipes will go on weeping into the joists, and the house will stand, and the house will not stand, and no one will come to fix the leak, because there is no leak, because the leak was never in the pipes, because the leak is him, has always been him, will always be him.

This is the madness.

It is not loud. It is not violent. It is a man in a hallway, looking at a man in a hallway, and the two of them, at last, are the same.

He finds himself, one evening, standing in the doorway of the kitchen the way David used to stand, with that small tilt of the head, and he catches his own reflection in the dark window and does not recognize which one of them is looking back.

Here is the part that no one tells you about going mad, which is that it is mostly waiting.

You wait for the figure to move. You wait for it to speak. You wait, in the small hours, for the moment when the eye slides toward the corner and the figure is closer than it was yesterday, or further, or changed in some way you cannot name but which you have memorized. You wait, and you do the dishes, and you go to work, and you come home, and the figure is there, and the waiting is over, and then begins again.

Marcus had thought, in the first days, that he was being punished. This is the natural thought. This is the thought of a man who still believes in a moral universe, who believes that the world keeps accounts, who believes that if he has done a thing then the thing will be done back to him, neatly, as a mirror does it.

But the figure is not a punishment. A punishment would end. A punishment would have a sentence, a release, a moment when the cell opens and the air outside smells different. The figure does not end. The figure is not a sentence. The figure is a climate.

Marcus is the climate. Marcus is the weather now. The guilt and the figure and the long slow rot of him have become a system, an ecosystem, a small closed world with its own laws, and he is the only animal in it, and he is both the predator and the prey, and the figure in the corner of his eye is neither, and is both, and is the only other thing alive.

On the night he finally looks directly at it, it is raining.

He doesn't plan it. He has spent six months not planning it, has built his whole life around the architecture of not, has become a man whose whole existence is a careful sideways sentence, a man who only ever looks at things from the corner, who only ever speaks to the room, who only ever acknowledges the world in the peripheral grammar of the unsaid.

But the rain is loud, and the apartment is small, and David is standing in the hallway again, and something in Marcus — some joist that has been weeping for months, some beam finally giving way — just turns.

He turns his whole head. He looks.

David is there.

He is exactly as he was. He is not translucent, which is the thing that surprises Marcus, the thing that the stories never got right. He is not a mist. He is not a suggestion. He is a man, standing in a hallway, in a perfectly ordinary apartment, on a perfectly ordinary night, and he looks at Marcus, and Marcus looks at him, and the rain is loud, and the light from the kitchen falls on David's face the way light has always fallen on faces, which is to say fully, which is to say without mercy.

David opens his mouth.

And the terrible thing, the thing that breaks the last of the beams, the thing that lets the ceiling finally come down — the terrible thing is that Marcus cannot tell, even now, whether David is about to speak or whether David has just spoken or whether David has been speaking, for six months, in a language Marcus has spent six months learning to almost-hear.

He will never know.

He will spend the rest of his life in the hallway. He will spend the rest of his life in the small warm climate of the rot. The figure will be there, and he will look at it, and the rain will be loud, and the light will fall, and somewhere in the walls the pipes will go on weeping into the joists, and the house will stand, and the house will not stand, and no one will come to fix the leak, because there is no leak, because the leak was never in the pipes, because the leak is him, has always been him, will always be him.

This is the madness.

It is not loud. It is not violent. It is a man in a hallway, looking at a man in a hallway, and the two of them, at last, are the same.

The snow came up to her shins now, each step a small surrender. Behind her, the pack had gone quiet—no more yipping, no more snapping branches. That was worse. That meant they were working it out among themselves, dividing the wood line into a crescent she couldn't see but could feel closing against her back like a fist.

She found the rock by accident, her calf slamming into it hard enough to buckle. When she turned, there was nothing behind her but white and the dark trunks of pines, and for one stupid, beautiful second she thought she'd lost them.

The first wolf came from the side she wasn't guarding.

No warning. One moment her shoulder was just her shoulder, packed under three layers of wool, and the next there was the sound—a sound like a wet canvas being torn—and a pressure so sudden and specific that for a fraction of a heartbeat her body couldn't even decide what had happened. Then the nerves caught up, and everything arrived at once.

The teeth went in just above the hip, where the pack strap of her satchel had rubbed the wool thin. She felt them pop through the fabric first, a strange, intimate series of small defeats, and then through the skin, which gave with less resistance than she'd imagined, less than a thought, and then a deeper, blunter pressure as they found the muscle. The wolf weighed maybe ninety pounds, and all ninety of them wrenched sideways at once, trying to drag her down, and the tearing inside her thigh was a thing she would later describe as *hot*—but in the moment, in the first second, it was none of those adjectives. It was just *loud*. A single bright note her body rang at, the way a bell rings, and she understood in that note, with a clarity she had never wanted, that the meat of her was a separate country from the rest of her, and she had just lost a border.

She screamed, or her mouth made a shape that was meant to be a scream, and the cold air took it and snapped it off short. Her hand found a branch. She swung, missed, swung again, felt the wood connect with something solid and warm, and the weight dropped away.

She made it three more steps before her leg stopped being a leg and became, instead, a thing she was carrying. Snow packed into the wound while she limped and the cold did something she hadn't expected—it didn't hurt less. It hurt in a different language, in long flat vowels of ache, while the bite itself kept shouting in the sharp consonants of broken blood. She put her hand against her hip without looking down and felt, under the frost already beading on her glove, a wet heat that seemed impossible out here, obscene, a small animal of warmth trying to escape through her fingers. The snow around her glove darkened in a pattern she could not stop making.

She kept moving. The blood kept moving. Somewhere ahead, she thought, there had to be a tree she could put her back to. The pack, behind her, had started up again—not running, not yet, just the soft crunch of paws in a body, patient, breathing, close enough now that she could smell them: wet fur and something older, something mineral, the same iron she could feel pumping out of herself and turning to steam in the air.

She did not look back. The cold followed her faithfully, as it always had, and the heat followed too, and she walked between them for as long as she could.

# The Hound of Meridian Station

Kira Vance crouched in the shadow of a rusted maintenance strut, her optical implants cycling through thermal overlays. The target — a corporate defector named Silas Crowe — was forty meters ahead, slipping through the derelict cargo bay like a man who'd done this before. He probably had.

"Target acquired," she subvocalized into the comms patch behind her ear. "Bay Seven, upper deck. He's running."

*Copy, Hound. Non-lethal preferred. Bond's tripled if you bring him in warm.* The dispatcher sounded bored. They always did.

Kira's boots whispered against the grated floor. Her chassis-suit — matte black polymer woven with myomer fibers — flexed with each step, amplifying her movement without betraying it. On her right hip, the *Lichtenberg VII* hummed softly in its holster. She'd named the stun weapon herself. The name felt appropriate.

Crowe reached a collapsed freight elevator and stopped. She watched him pull a small device from his sleeve — some kind of jammer, probably, the kind black-market techs built to scramble targeting systems and neural implants alike. Smart. The kind of smart that cost a lot of lives before someone hired her.

He never saw her drop from the strut.

She landed behind him in a crouch, and before he could spin, her left hand closed around his wrist, twisting it behind his back. "Silas Crowe. You're bonded to the Veritas Consortium. I'm collecting."

Crowe twisted, surprisingly strong for a desk-bound analyst. He drove an elbow back into her ribs, and though the suit absorbed most of it, the impact still sent a flash of white through her vision. He wrenched free, swinging the jammer at her face like a club. She leaned back, letting it whistle past, and kicked the back of his knee.

He dropped. But he didn't stay down.

He came up with a slender knife — monomolecular edge, the kind that could part a chassis-suit like paper if he found a seam. She parried with her forearm, felt the blade skate across reinforced polymer, and went for the Lichtenberg.

Crowe caught the movement. His eyes went wide, then calculating. "Vance. The Hound." He spat the name. "You know what they do to people who go back to Veritas, right? You know what I took?"

"I know what you cost them. Thirty million credits of proprietary cognitive research walked out of Sublevel Nine with you. That's why I'm here." She circled. "Come quietly. I don't want to use the L-seven."

"I don't want to be vivisected in a black-site operating theater. Funny how we both want things."

He lunged. Fast — faster than his file suggested. The knife drew a thin red line across her cheek before she got her forearm up and locked his wrist. They struggled, his face inches from hers, breath sour with fear-chemical.

She thumbed the safety off.

The Lichtenberg VII fired on contact — two prongs sinking through his jacket, through the dermis beneath, and into the muscle of his shoulder. The weapon discharged a pulsed, polyphase current at approximately fifty thousand volts, modulated at a frequency designed to interfere with the nervous system's own electrical signaling.

The effect on Crowe's body was immediate and total.

Every voluntary muscle fired at once. His back arched, his jaw clenched so hard she heard teeth meet, and his fingers splayed wide as the flexor and extensor muscles of his hand locked in simultaneous tetanic contraction. The knife dropped from fingers he could no longer command. A sound came out of him that wasn't quite a scream — the diaphragm was seizing too, so what emerged was a sharp, strangled bark as the air was forced from his lungs.

His eyes rolled. The pupils dilated, then fixed. The current wasn't strong enough to stop his heart, but it scrambled the signal cascade from brain to body, overwhelming the motor neurons with noise. Sensory neurons fired indiscriminately — pain, heat, pressure, all of it, none of it, a wash of meaningless static that the brain interpreted as white agony.

He collapsed, but the current kept him conscious. That was the cruel design of the L-seven: the body was hijacked, the mind trapped inside it, fully aware.

Kira held the trigger for the prescribed two-point-five seconds and released. Crowe crumpled to the deck, every muscle fiber exhausted from the involuntary contraction, his breathing ragged and shallow. Small burns marked the entry points of the prongs, pale pink welts that would darken to purple by morning. The rest of his body twitched in micro-spasms, aftershocks of the neural overload.

"Two-point-five," she said into the comms. "Target's down. Sending medical tag for the burn sites. He'll be conscious in a minute, but he won't be running anywhere for six hours."

She holstered the Lichtenberg and crouched beside him, sliding restraints over his wrists. His eyes were open, wet, fixed on the deck above. As the feeling came back, he'd feel the deep, bone-itching ache of muscle fatigue, the tingling of returning sensation in his fingertips, and the particular humiliation of having his body used against him.

She hauled him to his feet. He didn't resist. There was nothing left to resist with.

"Silas," she said, gentler than she usually allowed herself. "Whatever you took from them, whatever they did to make you run — that's between you and a court now. I'm just the leash."

He laughed weakly. It came out like a cough.

"Tell yourself that, Hound."

She did. Every night.

# The Reckoning Aboard the *Black Vengeance*

The plank stretched out from the *Black Vengeance* like a pale, accusing finger pointing into the void. Eight feet of weathered oak, lashed to the rail by ropes the bosun had secured mere minutes ago, hung suspended above a sea that had turned the color of a bruise—deep indigo churned to froth by the corpse-stiff wind.

Below, they circled.

Their shadows moved first, sleek and predatory, gliding through the water with a patience that only ancient hunger could teach. A flash of gray belly, a glimpse of black, dead eye, a fin knifing the surface with the precision of a razor's edge. Three of them now. Perhaps four. The crew had seen larger shadows drift past the hull in darker waters, creatures the old sailors whispered about in ports where the rum flowed and the talk grew tall.

Captain Draven Blackwood stood with his back to the horizon, the dying sun bleeding crimson behind his shoulders, and regarded the man on the plank with a gaze that held neither rage nor pity. He had used up both years ago. What remained was the cold arithmetic of command.

"Thomas Galloway," the Captain said, his voice carrying the way a storm carries thunder—low, inevitable. "You were found guilty by the Articles of Agreement, signed by your own hand, of conspiring with the navigator Brecklin to seize this vessel and turn her over to the British. He began to weep—not quietly, not with dignity, but the raw, hitching sobs of a child woken from a nightmare into a worse one. His bladder failed him, and a dark stain spread across his breeches, and he did not seem to notice, because he was watching the water, because the water was watching back.

# **Countdown**

The first thing is the wrongness of it—a bulk beneath his shirt that hadn't been there before, a strange heaviness across his sternum like a second heart, except this one didn't beat. It *buzzed*.

His fingers find it before his mind does. Cotton. Then something harder. Then a strap, nylon, biting into the soft flesh under his arms. His hands freeze there, hovering over the shape, and for three full seconds he refuses to know what it is.

*It's not what you think.*

He pulls the shirt up.

The device sits against his skin like a sleeping animal. Black polymer casing, scuffed at the corners, a battery pack duct-taped to one side. Wires—four of them, maybe five—red, blue, yellow, one bare copper strand that loops in a loose question mark against his pale stomach. He can feel them, the way you'd feel the legs of an insect. Cool. Slightly oily. The copper one has teeth where the insulation has been stripped away. One of them pricks the skin just below his left nipple and he flinches, a full-body jerk that makes the whole thing shift against his ribs.

*Oh God. Oh God oh God oh God.*

The ticking starts before he's ready for it. Or maybe it was always ticking and he just couldn't hear it over his own breathing. Now he can hear nothing else. A mechanical heartbeat, metronomic, *tick-tick-tick*, each one a small hard *pop* against the inside of his skull. Fast. Too fast. Or maybe that's his pulse. He can no longer tell which rhythm belongs to him.

His hands start to shake. This is the part no one tells you about—not the explosion, but the *shaking*. It begins in his fingertips, a tremor like Parkinson's, and climbs up through his wrists and into his forearms. He watches his own fingers dance above the wires and thinks, absurdly, *don't touch them, don't touch them, you'll know which one to cut, just like in the movies*—and then he laughs, a high, broken, airless sound that comes out of him like steam from a cracked pipe.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

He swallows. His mouth has gone dry and pasty, the inside of his cheeks stuck to his teeth. When he breathes, the air tastes metallic. He tries to peel the strap back and his fingers slip, sweaty, on the nylon. The device *sags* against him as he lifts the adhesive, and something inside it—some little mechanical thing—clicks, and he makes a noise he has never in his life made before, an animal keen, a sound that lives below language, and his bladder lets go, just a little, hot against his thigh, and he doesn't care, he doesn't *care*—

*Breathe. Breathe. You have to breathe.*

He tries to count the wires. One. Two. Three. The red one is thicker. That means something. That has to mean something. The yellow one disappears into the casing. The blue one is frayed at the end where someone's wire-strippers slipped. He is going to die because a stranger's wire-strippers *slipped*. The thought is so stupid, so cosmically unfair, that it sends him sideways into a laugh that turns into a sob that turns into a scream that he swallows before it can escape, because what if the screaming jostles something, what if the scream is the thing that kills him—

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

The room is very quiet. Somewhere outside, a car passes. A bird. A world going about its business, indifferent, and he wants to claw his way out of his own body, wants to climb out of this skin and leave the device behind like a shed snakeskin, but it is *on* him, it is *part* of him now, the ticking has synced with his pulse and he cannot tell where he ends and it begins. His hands hover over the wires. The copper one pricks him again. He watches a bead of blood well up, fat and slow, and roll down his stomach, and the ticking grows louder, and louder, and louder, and his thoughts are coming apart at the seams like the yellow wire's insulation, and somewhere, very far away, a voice that might still be his is saying *please please please please please*—

*Tick.*

*Tick.*

*Tick.*

# The Last Sound in the House

The house breathed differently at night. During the day, it was just a house—creaky floors, thin walls, the hum of the refrigerator. But after midnight, the settling sounds became footsteps. The drafts became breathing. The shadows became shapes that shifted when you weren't looking directly at them.

Mara knew this. She'd grown up in this house. She knew the sixteenth stair from the top always groaned. She knew the hallway between the bedrooms held a draft that came in from the window her father never fixed. She knew these things, and that was supposed to make it easier.

It didn't.

She had come back for the photo album. Just the album. In and out. Forty minutes, tops.

The power had gone out somewhere around 11 p.m.—a storm, the neighbors had said, trees down on Maple. Mara had stood in the kitchen with her phone flashlight for a long moment, weighing the choice, before deciding she wasn't going to leave without the album. Her mother was fading. The album mattered.

Now the phone was at twelve percent. She'd turned the brightness down, but the small white circle of light it cast felt obscene in the dark, a beacon announcing her to every corner of the house. She cupped her hand around it the way people did in movies, and felt foolish, and kept doing it anyway.

The stairs were the worst part.

She stood at the bottom and looked up. The darkness above was thick, almost physical, like something she could push her hand into. The air was colder up there—she could feel it drifting down, carrying the smell of old wood and something else, something faintly metallic that she didn't want to think about.

*One step at a time. You know this house. You know this house.*

The fourth step creaked. She winced. The eighth was silent. The twelfth—

The twelfth *groaned*, longer than it should have, as if the house were stretching beneath her.

She froze, listening.

Nothing. Just the storm outside, and the particular silence of a house holding its breath.

She climbed the rest of the way in quick, small steps, more of a controlled fall than a walk, and then she was in the upstairs hallway, and the dark was worse up here. Her mother's old bedroom door was open six inches. The guest bathroom door was closed. The door to her old room—

The door to her old room was closed, and she was certain, *certain*, she had left it open.

She stood very still.

The house settled somewhere in the walls. A small, soft sound. Could be pipes. Could be temperature shifts in old wood. Could be anything.

*Could be anything.*

She took a breath. Made herself move. Her old room was at the end of the hall, the photo album was on the shelf by the window, she could be in and out in under a minute. She kept her phone light low, kept her hand cupped over it, and she walked, and she did not look at the guest bathroom door as she passed it.

She looked at the guest bathroom door.

It was just a door.

*Just a door.*

She made it to her old room. Pushed the door open. The hinges didn't make a sound this time, and somehow that was worse. The room was full of the shapes she remembered—the outline of the bed, the dresser, the old desk chair with the broken arm—but everything was rearranged, slightly, into something unrecognizable. Her brain kept trying to map the old geography and failing.

She found the shelf by feel more than sight. Her fingers walked along the spines of old books, a ceramic cat she'd forgotten about, and then—the album. The worn cloth cover, the soft give of it under her fingers. She tucked it under her arm.

That was when she heard it.

Not a sound. The *absence* of a sound. A pocket of stillness in the house, somewhere behind her, as if something had stopped moving at the same moment she had.

She didn't turn around.

*If you turn around, you'll see something. If you see something, you have to decide what to do about it. If you don't see it, you can still tell yourself it was nothing.*

She took a step toward the door.

Behind her, the faintest displacement of air. A smell—warm, human, the copper-and-salt smell of skin. The softest possible whisper of fabric against fabric, like a sleeve drawn back along an arm, the small preparatory movement of a hand adjusting its grip.

Mara's phone died.

The dark came down instantly, total and absolute, and in that dark, somewhere very close to her, a man she had never seen began to breathe again, deliberately, as if he had been holding it, as if he had been waiting for exactly this.

The last thing she heard, before she opened her mouth to scream, was a small, soft, patient sound—

The click of a blade being opened.

The scene in the trench is one of immediate and overwhelming panic, compounded by the body's violent revolt against the poison.

**The Onset:**
The first warning is not always visual—often it's a smell, a sharp, acrid tang of chlorine or the cloying, sweetish scent of phosgene. Soldiers may see a yellowish-green cloud rolling low along the trench floor, heavier than air, pooling into the low places where men crouch. The instinct is to gasp, and that first desperate inhalation is often the most damaging.

**Physical Symptoms:**
The respiratory system attacks itself in a cascading failure:

- **Immediate burning:** The mucous membranes of the nose, throat, and lungs ignite with a searing, corrosive pain. It feels like inhaling hot embers or ground glass. The eyes swell, tear profusely, and vision blurs.
- **Drowning in air:** Fluid begins leaking into the alveoli of the lungs. The soldier is, in essence, suffocating in his own bodily fluid. Each breath becomes a wet, rattling struggle—a gurgling, liquid sound audible to those nearby.

# The Sitting Room

The study smelled of Cuban tobacco and old leather. Vincent DeLuca didn't look up from the chessboard when Marco entered. He moved a bishop, captured a pawn, and set the piece down with a soft click before finally raising his eyes.

"Sit."

Marco sat. The chair was a leather wingback, deep enough to swallow a man. He kept his hands on his knees, palms down. You don't put your hands in your pockets in Vincent's presence. You don't fidget. You don't breathe too loudly.

"Tell me about Sal."

Marco cleared his throat. "He's been meeting with the Marchetti family. Twice in the last week. I have photographs."

Vincent studied the board. He picked up a knight, turned it slowly between his thick fingers, and set it back down without moving it.

"And what did our friend have to say for himself?"

"He says they were just talking business. Restaurant supplies."

"Restaurant supplies." Vincent almost smiled. "Sal was always a poor liar. It's one of the things I liked about him." He exhaled a thin stream of smoke toward the ceiling. "He delivered my daughter's wedding cake, you know. Personally. Drove it across town in the rain. That's the kind of man I thought I was dealing with."

A long silence. The grandfather clock in the hall measured it out in slow, expensive ticks.

"Does he know we know?"

"I don't think so, boss."

"Good. I'd hate to frighten him." Vincent took another drag. The cherry flared. "I'd hate for Sal to spend his last few days looking over his shoulder. A man should be able to enjoy his time."

Marco said nothing. He knew this rhythm. Vincent liked to wind the clock himself before handing it to you.

"You know, Marco, when my father took me into the business, he told me something I never forgot. He said, *'Vincent, a garden doesn't grow by itself. You have to prune the dead branches. Otherwise the whole thing rots.'*"

He tapped ash into a crystal tray.

"Sal is a dead branch."

Another silence. He moved the knight at last — a strange, almost playful move, sacrificing it for nothing.

"I want him gone by Sunday. He's a family man, so do it at home. His wife shouldn't have to wonder. And Marco —" Vincent's eyes finally settled on him, dark and patient as old wells. "Make sure he understands *why*. I want him to know exactly what he did. Then I want it to be over quickly. He's a man who once did me a kindness, and I am not without sentiment."

Marco stood. "Consider it done."

"Marco."

He stopped at the door.

"The Marchetti family. After Sal... I want you to send them a gift. A nice one. Something they can put on their table." Vincent paused. "And tell them if they ever *shop* in my garden again, I won't be so generous with the pruning shears."

"Of course, boss."

"Close the door on your way out."

Marco did. In the hallway he loosened his collar, took his first real breath in fifteen minutes, and reached for his phone. The number he dialed was one he kept memorized — no contacts, no history, no paper trail.

When a man answered, Marco said only:

"Sunday. The house. He'll be expecting company."

He hung up and walked out into the cold night, where the city hummed along, indifferent as always to the small, quiet transactions that kept it running.

# The Weight of Silence

The first sound is the absence of sound. The world above—birdsong, wind, the distant murmur of mourners—severs itself cleanly, like a thread pulled taut until it snaps. Then comes the *thud*. The first spadeful of earth strikes the lid, and Marcus understands with a clarity that burns through him that this is not a dream, not a trance, not the cruel trick of a sleeping mind.

Another thud. The coffin shivers beneath him, and the lanterns of his thoughts flare wildly in the dark.

**Air.** The thought arrives like a fist. *How much air? How much air is in this box, how much air is in this box, how much—* He drags in a breath that tastes of velvet and pine sap and the faintly sweet undertone of his own terror-sweat. The air is a finite thing now. A glass of water being poured out, drop by drop, and no way to refill it.

The walls press inward, though he knows—*knows*—they are not moving. Six feet of length. Eighteen inches of width. His arms cannot lie flat. His shoulders, when he tries to stretch them, brush the lid above and the floor below. The wood is cool at first, then becomes the temperature of his body, and somehow this is worse—the casket drinking him in, swallowing his warmth, becoming an extension of his flesh.

Another thud. Closer. The earth is settling around the box, and with each percussion the lid seems to grow heavier, though it cannot—the wood is the same wood, the nails the same nails. But the *weight* above him is a living thing, a great gray hand pressing down, down, down. He feels the soil creep into every joint and seam of the coffin, hears the soft intimate whisper of it finding every crack through which light will never come.

**The dark is not empty.** It teems. His eyes, straining, paint phantoms on the black—faces, hands, the pale oval of his mother's face as she lay in her coffin, and he was seven, and he had leaned in to kiss her, and her eyes had been closed, closed, closed—

He screams. The sound is a wet, muffled thing, swallowed almost before it leaves his throat. He screams again, and the noise is a mockery, a thing for insects.

His hands find the lid. The wood is smooth, polished, an obscenity of craftsmanship—someone had *finished* this box, had sanded it, had lacquered it, had fitted a little pillow of silk for his head. He claws. Fingernails skid across the satin, catch on the grain, bend back, and the pain is exquisite, is *real*, and he claws harder because the pain proves he is not dead, not dead, *not dead yet*.

Above him, thud after thud after thud. The weight is immense now. It is the weight of continents. His arms tremble, and the muscles in his shoulders are small burning things, and his fingers are bleeding, and the wood is *so smooth*, and the nails beneath his nails are an inch of solid oak, and the earth above the oak is six feet of eternity.

He rolls onto his side. He cannot breathe. He *can* breathe. He cannot breathe. His chest is a bellows being crushed. The air is thinner now, or he is thicker with panic, and each breath is a theft, a borrowing, a thing he must repay with interest soon.

*Let me out.* The thought is a child's thought, a prayer-shaped thing, useless as the clawing, useless as the screaming, useless as the air. *Let me out, let me out, I was not ready, I am not done, I have not—*

Thud.

Thud.

Thud.

The dirt, settling, shifts. A fine powder sifts through a seam near his face, warm and intimate as breath, and it tastes of iron and root. He opens his mouth to scream and the dirt enters him, and he chokes, and he claws, and the wood holds, and the dark is now complete—not merely dark, but *populated*, a dark that has a texture, a weight, a hunger.

His fingers slow. The bleeding has stopped, or has not. He cannot tell. He rests his cheek against the lid and feels, somewhere above, the faintest vibration of a final spadeful being leveled smooth.

Grass, perhaps. The sound of someone walking away.

The weight is everything. The weight is the world. He is beneath it, and the air is a coin in a closed hand, and the dark is a thing that is learning his name.

# The Seventh Round

The left eye was gone. Not closed — *gone*, swallowed whole by a purple hemorrhage that stretched from brow to cheekbone, the lid puffed up like a ruptured plum. Blood had seeped into the sclera, turning the white of his eye into a sickly marbled map of broken vessels. He could only see the world now through a pinhole of clarity in his right eye, everything else drowned in that swelling, crimson fog.

His mouthpiece hung loose, slick with saliva and something copper. A cut above the left brow wept freely, the blood tracking down his face in thin tributaries, cutting channels through the sweat and vaseline until it dripped from his jaw onto the canvas in a slow, metronome patter. *Tap. Tap. Tap.*

Then came the body shot.

A short, chopping right hook that burrowed under the elbow, finding the soft tissue between the floating ribs and the hip. The sound arrived a half-second after the impact — a wet, wooden *crack*, like a branch snapping over a knee. Not the sharp pop of a hand meeting flesh, but something deeper, something structural giving way. The kind of sound that makes cornermen flinch and ringside physicians reach for their stopwatch.

The fighter's body folded around the pain, knees buckling inward as if his skeleton had simply forgotten how to hold him upright. Air came out in a thin, reedy whistle — not a scream, because there wasn't enough air left for that, just the involuntary gasp of a lung trying to find room to expand around a rib that was no longer where it belonged. He stumbled forward, not retreating, because retreat requires energy and he'd spent his somewhere around the fourth.

His legs moved in that strange, stilted marionette walk of a man operating on courage rather than capacity. The crowd could see it — the slight hitch, the way his left hand dropped a half-beat late on the jab, the way he leaned into his opponent now not to throw but simply to stay vertical. His corner screamed instructions he could no longer process. *Move your head. Move your head.* But the head moved on its own now, lolling slightly between his shoulders like something loosely tethered.

The other fighter saw it. That recognition passed between them — predator and prey in the same bright square of canvas — and another hook came, then another, each one finding the same cracked infrastructure, the fractured rib now grinding against its neighbor with every breath. The damaged fighter's face had taken on a waxy, distant quality, the eyes glassy and unfocused, seeing something past his opponent, past the lights, past the ropes.

The towel would come in forty seconds. The commission would suspend him. The doctors would find the broken rib, the detached retina beginning its slow work, the orbital fracture they wouldn't discover until the CT scan three days later.

But right now, in the seventh round, he was still standing — and that was the cruelest thing of all.

# The Last Cup

The drawing room of Ashworth Manor held its breath. Late November light, gray as a mourning veil, pressed against the tall windows, finding the polished silver of the teapot and the lace at Mrs. Eleanor Ashworth's cuffs. She poured. Her hands did not tremble.

Charles lifted the cup to his lips. He smiled at her over the rim—that small, private smile he reserved for the two of them, the one that had undone her fifteen years ago at a garden party in Kent. He drank.

She watched him set the cup down, watched the muscle along his jaw work as he swallowed. For a moment, nothing. Outside, a carriage passed on the gravel drive, and somewhere deep in the house a clock marked the quarter hour. Then Charles's brow furrowed. He pressed a hand to his stomach.

"Eleanor."

His voice was strange. Thin. She remained seated, her teacup steady in her own hands, and watched as the first beads of sweat gathered at his temples despite the chill of the room.

"My dear, I—" He rose halfway from his chair, then fell back. A violent retching seized him, and he clapped a hand to his mouth. His face had gone the color of tallow. The veins in his neck stood out like cords as he doubled forward, a dry heave that produced nothing at first, then brought up a thin stream of bile tinged pink.

"Ring for—" he began, but another spasm took him, and the words dissolved into a groan. His bowels loosened then. The smell reached her before the sound did—a foulness, sour and metallic, that had nothing to do with the lavender she had burned in the grate that morning.

Charles slid from his chair onto the Axminster carpet, his fingers clawing at the roses woven there. He vomited again, and this time there was blood in it, dark and congealed. A terrible thirst seemed to overtake him. He crawled toward the sideboard where a decanter of water stood, but his legs would not obey him. They had begun to cramp, the muscles of his calves knotting beneath his trousers, drawing his feet into grotesque arches. He made a sound—half a sob, half a scream—as the cramps climbed into his thighs.

Eleanor set her teacup into its saucer. *Click.* The sound was very small.

His eyes found hers across the room. They were wide now, the pupils enormous and black. The whites had taken on a yellowish cast, and fine threads of red were bursting across them, as if the vessels within had surrendered all at once. His lips, which had been pale, were going blue. He tried to speak. A frothy saliva gathered at the corners of his mouth, and when he drew breath, it came in shallow, ragged draws, as though the air itself had grown thick and poisonous.

"Eleanor. *Eleanor.* What—"

The convulsions began without warning. His back arched, his hands splayed and rigid, the fingers curved like claws. He struck his head against the leg of the sideboard. Once. Twice. A dark line of blood traced itself down his temple and pooled against the wood.

She rose then, slowly, and moved toward the bellpull. Perhaps she would summon the housemaid. Perhaps she would simply stand in the window and watch the carriage lamps go out along the lane, one by one, as the household went quiet. Perhaps there was a letter, already written and sealed, in the drawer of her writing desk—words set down in the careful copperplate of a woman who had planned every particular of the evening, down to the hour, down to the steam that had risen from his cup as she carried it to him.

Charles's body had begun to quiet. The convulsions subsided into tremors. He lay on his side now, his breath coming in long, wet rattles, each one a little softer than the last. The sweat had soaked through his collar. His bowels had failed entirely, and he lay in the ruin of himself, his gaze still fixed on her face with an expression she would carry, she knew, into whatever room she walked into for the rest of her life.

Not accusation, precisely. Something worse. *Recognition.*

The last breath went out of him with a sound like a sigh, and the clock in the hall chimed the half hour, and Eleanor Ashworth reached, at last, for the bellpull, and pulled.

# The Rationer's Due

The pit smelled of rust and old rain.

Mara stood across from the man she'd never seen before yesterday, when they'd both been chosen from the Stacks. The crowd above the corrugated rim pressed against the floodlights, their faces pale smudges in the glare. Some were cheering. Most were quiet, waiting to see who their neighbors would be eating with this week.

The system was elegant, in its way. The Council had stopped pretending the old economy existed. Now everything ran on Bellies Fed. A fight in the pit meant twelve weeks of full rations for the winner. Nothing for the loser, of course, except the dignity of having freed up another mouth.

The man across from her—Jules, someone had whispered his name—held a length of rebar with a strip of cloth wrapped around one end for grip. She had the same. Standard issue. The Council wasn't in the business of making it easy, but they weren't making it impossible either. They wanted shows, not suicides.

He was taller than her. Younger, maybe. His hands were shaking, which told her everything she needed to know about how many pits he'd fought in before.

*None*, she realized. *This is his first.*

She'd killed once before, eight months back. A woman named Petra who'd had three children waiting in the Stacks. Mara still dreamed about the way Petra had looked at her in the last moment—not with hatred, but with something worse. Understanding.

*You did what you had to*, those eyes had said. *And now I'll do what I have to, which is nothing, ever again.*

The buzzer sounded.

Jules came in high, desperate, the rebar whistling. She stepped aside and let his momentum carry him past. He stumbled, caught himself, turned. She could see him trying to find the monster inside himself, the thing the pit was supposed to grow. He was looking for it the way a man looks for a light switch in a dark room.

He didn't have one. He was just a boy.

Mara circled. The crowd's murmur rose and fell like surf. Somewhere above, a man was selling roasted chickpeas at a markup only the winners could afford.

"I'm sorry," Jules said, almost to himself.

She came in low this time, feinting at his knees, then rising. He parried, barely. The rebar sang. They traded two more exchanges—testing, measuring—and she felt him begin to tire. The pit wasn't a place you lasted long if you fought afraid.

On the fourth pass, he lunged. She caught his bar with hers, locked them, and stepped inside his reach. For a half-second they were close enough to share breath. She saw his eyes—brown, wet, the eyes of someone who had not yet learned to make a small room of his chest and live in it.

She put the tip of her rebar into the soft place just below his sternum and leaned, the way you'd lean into a heavy door, and the world went quiet on him.

It wasn't dramatic. That was the part the songs never got right. He didn't cry out. He looked down at her hands, surprised, the way a person looks down when they've forgotten their coat. Then he folded, gently, the way a coat would fold, and the ground took him.

The crowd made its small, satisfied noise. Somewhere a bell rang. A ration chit dropped into her slot at the gate.

Mara stood over Jules for a long moment, her rebar still in her hands. The floodlights were very bright, and very white, and they made the world look clean, which was the worst part of all, because the world had not been clean for a long time.

She walked out of the pit carrying twelve weeks of flour and the look on a dead man's face, and she did not once let herself run, because running was for people who still believed they could get somewhere.

**The Reckoning on Route 7**

Maya's knuckles were white on the steering wheel, her eyes darting between the rearview mirror and the rain-slicked highway unfurling before her. The black SUV was closing again—maybe forty meters back now—and the muzzle flash from its passenger window came a half-second before the *crack* that shattered her passenger-side mirror into a web of fractured glass.

She didn't think. She reacted.

Her right hand left the wheel just long enough to draw the Glock from between her thighs, and she fired three blind shots through the shattered window without looking. The recoil jolted up her arm, a familiar tremor that, somewhere beneath the roaring in her ears, felt almost comforting. The SUV swerved. She floored the accelerator.

A delivery truck loomed in her lane. She yanked the wheel left, tires screaming, and shot through a gap that shouldn't have existed—between a minivan and a sedan, close enough that she heard the mother in the minivan scream, saw the child's face pressed wide-eyed against the rear window, saw the little mouth open in a soundless O.

The world had narrowed to a tunnel of immediate sensation: the smell of burnt rubber, the taste of copper, the frantic percussion of her own heartbeat in her throat. Everything else was mathematics. Distance. Angle. Closing speed. The lives around her reduced, horrifyingly, to variables—obstacles to avoid or, worse, obstacles to use as cover.

She cut hard right, forcing the SUV to brake as she threaded between a bus and a taxi. Somewhere a horn screamed, long and sustained. A pedestrian on the median dove for the guardrail as her car whipped past, the slipstream nearly pulling the man off his feet.

*Get out. Get out. Get out.*

But the highway was a chain, and she was only as fast as the cars in front of her. A school bus had appeared two lanes over, crawling up an on-ramp. Thirty children in yellow vests, visible through every window. The SUV didn't care. She could see the gun barrel tracking her, and she understood, with a clarity that felt almost peaceful, that if she braked now they would ram her, and if they rammed her here, the bus would take the hit.

So she floored it instead.

The engine screamed. The speedometer blurred past numbers she refused to read. She fired twice more, just to make them flinch, just to buy herself a single precious second, and then she saw it—the off-ramp, the cloverleaf, the escape into the industrial maze of the waterfront.

She took it at seventy miles an hour, the car bottoming out, sparks showering behind her like a dying star. In the mirror, the SUV committed to the turn, tires shrieking, and she allowed herself one ragged breath.

Her hands were shaking. She had nearly killed a child. She had nearly killed a mother. She had used their bodies as instruments of her survival, and she could still see the little face at the window, still see the open mouth, and the breath turned to ash in her lungs.

The Glock felt heavier than it had all night.

Ahead, the warehouses rose like tombstones against the bruised sky, and she drove toward them with the desperate, terrified certainty that whatever she was running from was nothing—*nothing*—compared to what she had already become.

The wooden edge of the table connects just above the brow, and the sound arrives before the pain—a hollow, percussive *thock* that seems to echo inside the skull rather than outside it.

For a half-second, there is nothing. A strange, floating absence, as if the mind has briefly stepped out of the room to consider the situation from a distance.

Then the world reassembles, but wrong.

**The senses rebel in sequence:**

- **Sight** comes back smeared. The fluorescent light overhead bleeds into a white halo. The interrogator's face swims in and out of focus, doubled at the edges. The table beneath has acquired a grainy, almost breathing texture.
- **Sound** arrives muffled, as though heard through a wall of water. A voice is speaking—low, patient, almost gentle—but the words lag a full second behind the moving lips, like a badly dubbed film.
- **Touch** is strange. There's a hot, tight band of pressure across the forehead, but the rest of the body feels distant, remote, belonging to someone else. The tongue is thick and unhelpful against the roof of the mouth.
- **Taste**—copper, unmistakable, pooling at the back of the throat where the bite of the impact was met by an involuntary clench of the jaw.

**The daze itself is a kind of terrible mercy.** Thoughts don't connect the way they should. A question is asked, and the answer surfaces somewhere, but the bridge between hearing and speaking has been damaged. There is a long, blank pause that feels normal from the inside—the character isn't aware of how much time has passed. To them, they answered immediately. To the officer, seconds have stretched into a small, satisfying silence.

**Physically**, the body has entered a kind of low-grade crisis: blood rushing away from the extremities, a fine tremor in the hands that the character tries and fails to hide, a ringing tone in the ears that flattens all other sound into a single narrow channel. Nausea hovers at the edges—not dramatic, not the kind that causes vomiting, but a queasy, grounding wrongness, the body's quiet insistence that something has been damaged.

**Emotionally**, the world has simplified. Fear is no longer abstract. It is the table. It is the hands. It is the question that will come again, because the silence has already told the officer that he has found the right pressure to apply.

When the next question finally arrives, the character's mouth is already working on an answer they don't remember deciding to give.

For a half-second, there is nothing. A strange, floating absence, as if the mind has briefly stepped out of the room to consider the situation from a distance.

Then the world reassembles, but wrong.

The senses rebel in sequence:

  • Sight comes back smeared. The fluorescent light overhead bleeds into a white halo. The interrogator's face swims in and out of focus, doubled at the edges. The table beneath has acquired a grainy, almost breathing texture.
  • Sound arrives muffled, as though heard through a wall of water. A voice is speaking—low, patient, almost gentle—but the words lag a full second behind the moving lips, like a badly dubbed film.
  • Touch is strange. There's a hot, tight band of pressure across the forehead, but the rest of the body feels distant, remote, belonging to someone else. The tongue is thick and unhelpful against the roof of the mouth.
  • Taste—copper, unmistakable, pooling at the back of the throat where the bite of the impact was met by an involuntary clench of the jaw.

The daze itself is a kind of terrible mercy. Thoughts don't connect the way they should. A question is asked, and the answer surfaces somewhere, but the bridge between hearing and speaking has been damaged. There is a long, blank pause that feels normal from the inside—the character isn't aware of how much time has passed. To them, they answered immediately. To the officer, seconds have stretched into a small, satisfying silence.

Physically, the body has entered a kind of low-grade crisis: blood rushing away from the extremities, a fine tremor in the hands that the character tries and fails to hide, a ringing tone in the ears that flattens all other sound into a single narrow channel. Nausea hovers at the edges—not dramatic, not the kind that causes vomiting, but a queasy, grounding wrongness, the body's quiet insistence that something has been damaged.

Emotionally, the world has simplified. Fear is no longer abstract. It is the table. It is the hands. It is the question that will come again, because the silence has already told the officer that he has found the right pressure to apply.

When the next question finally arrives, the character's mouth is already working on an answer they don't remember deciding to give.

# The Whisper of the Bolt

Elira's lungs burned as she crashed through the underbrush, tearing her cloak on a low-hanging branch that clawed at her face like skeletal fingers. The forest was a black cathedral of pine and shadow, its columns rising into a canopy so dense the moon existed only as a rumor somewhere far above. She couldn't see her own feet. She could barely see the hand she held in front of her.

But she could *hear*.

Not the owl, distant and indifferent. Not the wind that hissed through the needles like breath between teeth. Something else. Something deliberate. A footfall, soft as a thought, somewhere behind her. To her left. Then—impossibly—*ahead* of her, before the sound vanished again, swallowed by the trees.

He was circling.

She stumbled over a root and went down hard, palms scraping against wet stone and pine needles. For a heartbeat she lay there, chest heaving, listening with every atom of her body. The forest listened back. Somewhere, water dripped. Somewhere, a branch creaked with the slow patience of a thing that had waited a thousand years.

She got up. She had to get up.

The thought of stopping—of simply lying down and letting whatever followed find her—bloomed in her mind like a dark flower, and she understood with sick clarity that this was how the forest killed you. Not the cold. Not the roots. The *surrender*. The sweet, whispering offer of rest.

She ran.

The path—if it had ever been a path—was gone. She moved by instinct now, by the half-remembered geography of a chase that had already lasted an hour or a lifetime, she no longer knew. The trees pressed closer. Their bark gleamed with moisture. The air tasted of moss and iron and her own fear, sour on the back of her tongue.

Then she heard it.

Not a footfall this time. Something thinner. Sharper. A sound like a drawn breath, like a single sustained note of a violin played by something that had learned music only to pervert it. A sound she felt before she understood—splitting the air, threading the dark, coming for her from a direction she hadn't thought to fear.

The bolt passed her right ear.

Close. *So close* she felt the wind of it—felt the displaced air kiss the fine hairs there, a lover's last breath against her neck. For a single impossible instant she could have reached out and plucked it from the air, could have felt the fletching tickle her fingers, could have turned to meet her hunter's eyes at last.

She did not turn. She *screamed*, and the scream became a sob, and the sob became motion, and she threw herself sideways into a hollow between two roots, curling into a ball of mud and terror. Her heart was no longer a heart; it was a fist, pounding on the inside of her ribs, demanding to be let out.

Silence.

No—not silence. The *other* silence. The listening kind. The kind that followed the bolt the way a shadow follows a blade.

He was close now. She could smell him—or thought she could, some ghost of leather and lamp oil and something older, something that smelled like the inside of a closed room in winter. She could hear his breathing. Or was it hers? She pressed her hand over her mouth, bit down on the meat of her thumb until she tasted blood.

*Why didn't it hit me?*

The thought arrived unbidden, terrible in its logic. He was good. She had known that since the first bolt had taken a chip of bark from a tree an inch from her cheek, back when she had still believed the forest would end, back when she had still thought this could be escaped. A man this good did not miss.

He was *aiming*.

Not for her body. Not yet. For the dark spaces just beside her, so that the whistling became its own kind of language, its own kind of instruction. *Here. I could have ended it here. And here. And here. See how patient I am. See how the world is full of almosts, full of the inches between your skin and the iron that loves it.*

A branch cracked, off to her right.

Elira closed her eyes. Behind her eyelids, the dark was the same as the dark in front of them, but somehow kinder. She could stop. She could lie very still and perhaps the arrow would find her heart cleanly, and the cold would come, and the forest would close above her like water, and she would not have to hear that sound again, that thin bright singing of the bolt, that almost-touch of death upon her skin.

But the fist in her chest beat on. Beat on. Beat on.

And somewhere ahead, so faint she might have imagined it, a light.

She opened her eyes.

She ran.

**Field of Crows**

The guns have gone to sleep. The silence spreads
across the churned and trembling earth,
and in the hush the small inheritors
come forth.

First, the flies—black beads upon the air,
singing their thin, unending hymn
to what the living left behind.
They do not mourn. They do not ask.
They settle on the open eyes
with the patience of a closing door.

Then, the crows,
heavy and deliberate as undertakers,
hopping among the fallen with a black,
businesslike concern—
tugging at the loose threads of a sleeve,
picking the silver from a tunic's seam,
stepping over hands that will not rise again.

A beetle turns the soil.
A single ant, industrious and blind,
begins the long arithmetic of bone.

The dead lie still.
They do not dream. They do not stir
when the carrion-bird alights
upon a chest that will not lift
or flutter at the touch of wind.
Their mouths are open to the sky,
but nothing answers. Nothing comes
but light, indifferent, falling equally
on friend, on foe, on the broken gun,
on the letter never sent,
on the name carved soft into a tree
some hundred miles from here, by someone's hand
that thought, *I'll come home to you.*

The grass will come. The grass always comes.
It will push through the rusted buckle,
through the splintered stock, the rotted flag,
the quiet mouths of those who fell
with courage in them, or with fear,
or only with the animal surprise
of breathing, and then breathlessness.

The birds will have their hour.
The insects, their slow appointment.
And after them, the patient green,
and after green, the men who come
with careful hands and numbered tags,
to do the work the scavengers
have left unfinished—
to learn, again, the names,
to whisper them into waiting earth,

as though to say: *you were not silence.
You were not stillness.
You were someone, once, who heard the morning
and was glad of it.*

But that is later. That is for tomorrow.

Now there is only this:
the field, the light, the low wind
stirring nothing,
and the crows,
the patient crows,
going about their work.
