# Carrion Claim

The dog's eyes caught the last of the dusk like two embers buried in filth. A Rottweiler, or what was left of one—the ribs a roadmap beneath matted fur, the jowls scarred and torn from a hundred forgotten fights. It had been tracking you since the overpass, drawn by the half-jar of pickled beets you'd been cradling against your chest like a newborn.

Six months ago, you would have run. Six months ago, you still had a name for what was happening to the world. Now you had a hand-rolled cigarette, a rusted hunting knife, and a stomach that had been eating itself for eleven days.

The dog crouched ten paces out, a low growl vibrating in its chest like an idling engine. It knew. They always knew. The weak ones, the slow ones, the ones whose bodies had begun to consume their own muscles for fuel. It could smell the ketones on your breath, the dissolution happening inside you.

You took a step back. It took a step forward.

Your left hand—shaking, the knuckles swollen, two fingernails blackened from frostbite—tightened around the jar. Your right drew the knife. The blade was dull. It had been dull for weeks. You hadn't found whetstone or oil in longer than you could remember, and the edge had been dulled further by scraping through rusted cans, by digging in frozen earth, by the three feral cats that had come for your water cache in October.

The dog lunged.

It was faster than you'd expected—faster than a thing that looked like a walking autopsy should be. Sixty pounds of hunger and muscle memory hitting you square in the chest. You went down hard, the back of your skull cracking against asphalt, the jar spinning from your grip, rolling under a rusted chassis three feet away.

Teeth found your forearm. Clamped. The pain was not sharp, exactly—it was *deep*, a hot, wet pressure that made you understand in your marrow that this creature intended to kill you. Not to eat you. To *take*. There was no negotiation in its eyes, no recognition, no kinship between mammal and mammal. Only arithmetic: there is food, and I am taking it.

You drove the knife into the soft place behind its jaw.

The dog's claws scrabbled against your ribs, shredding the last good shirt you owned. Its growl turned into a wet, bubbling snarl, and the grip of its teeth somehow tightened as the blade twisted. You felt the pop of cartilage, the hot gush of something vital against your wrist. It was the smell that would stay with you—the copper-and-feces reek of an animal's last argument, made at the volume of a scream.

You rolled. Pinned it. The dog's remaining legs kicked against the pavement in a rhythm that slowed like a clock winding down. Its eyes, those ember eyes, found yours. For one moment—just one, before the light left them—you saw something you had not seen in another living creature in longer than you could measure.

*Recognition.*

Not of you. Of itself. Of the thing it had been before the world ended, before the food ran out, before the owners who once fed it from ceramic bowls put a bullet in its sibling and left it to fend in the ruins. You saw the memory of a soft hand, a backyard, a tennis ball thrown in summer.

Then it was gone. The legs stopped.

You lay on the cold asphalt for a long time, breathing through your mouth, your forearm screaming, the sky a bruised purple overhead. When you finally crawled to the chassis, the jar was still there. One of the beets had rolled out, and you picked it up in your blood-slicked fingers and ate it from the ground, dirt and all, and it was the sweetest thing you had ever tasted, and you hated yourself for how desperately you wanted another.

The dog was still warm when you dragged yourself away.

You didn't look back.

# The Worst Kind of House Call

The rain had stopped two hours ago, but the mud still remembered it. Martinez lay propped against a fallen log, his camo jacket peeled back to reveal a hole just below the left shoulder that pulsed with each breath—dark, wet, impossibly deep. The entry wound was small, almost polite. The exit was not.

"Tell me again," Jensen said, rolling up his sleeves to the elbows. His hands were already shaking. They hadn't stopped shaking since the ambush.

"Through and through," Martinez managed. His teeth were bared, his face the color of tallow. "Skipped off the collarbone, maybe. Feels like... like someone poured hot oil in there."

Jensen could see the blood welling in a slow, stubborn rhythm—not the arterial spray that meant death in minutes, but the steady leak that meant death in hours. Hours they didn't have. The LZ was still forty klicks north, and the volume of fire had moved east, which meant either the column was coming, or the whole battalion was gone.

He laid out his tools on a piece of torn poncho. The bayonet from his ruined pack—six inches of carbon steel, the edge still factory-new. A leather belt, doubled over, for Martinez to bite. A ballpoint pen and a length of 550 cord, for a makeshift suture. The bottle of Bushmills, three-quarters full, had cost him a pack of smokes and a promise to a dead lieutenant. Now it was the most valuable thing in the I Corps.

"This is going to be bad," he said, because he had promised himself he would never lie to Martinez.

"I know, doc. Just... not the shoulder, man. My pitching arm."

Despite everything, Jensen barked a laugh that came out sounding like a cough. He poured a long measure of whiskey over the blade. Then he poured the rest, every golden drop, directly into the wound.

Martinez screamed. The sound was animal, high, the kind of scream that lives in the ribs of anyone who hears it for the rest of their life. His back arched, and Jensen had to drop the bottle to pin him down with one forearm across the chest. Blood fountained up around his wrist, hot as soup, slippery as oil. Martinez bit down on the belt, and the sound it made when his teeth locked was the sound of a man trying to swallow his own tongue.

"Hold him," Jensen said to no one. He was alone. He had been alone for the better part of an hour.

He pinched the wound edges open with his left hand—god, the *give* of it, the way the muscle parted like something alive and unwilling—and slid the bayonet in. results.model_response:
# Crossfire

The first shot cracked like a branch snapping in winter, and then the world turned to noise and glass.

Inside the bank, the air itself seemed to fracture. Teller windows exploded inward in a cascade of glittering shards, each one catching the fluorescent light for a single frozen instant before tumbling through the thick, choking smoke of discharged powder. The smell was acrid, metallic, the bite of cordite mixing with the copper-and-sweat tang of panic.

From the vault corridor, Danny Voss had the shot lined up clean—a clean line of sight through the shattered frame of the manager's office, past the toppled potted fern, straight to the officer ducking behind a marble planter. He squeezed.

But by then the geometry of the room had betrayed him.

A slug from a patrol rifle punched through the drywall above his head, spraying him with a fine mist of chalky plaster. Splinters of the doorframe peppered his cheek. Somewhere to his left, Marisol was screaming something—*move, move, MOVE*—but her voice was swallowed by the rolling thunder of return fire, a sustained roar that made the floor vibrate beneath his boots. Bullets chewed into the marble counter, sending white chips skittering across the tile like broken teeth.

The hostages were a problem. They'd scattered like startled birds, some behind the overturned tables, one woman curled fetal beneath the writing desk, and every one of them a potential screen—or worse, a witness with a clear view of faces. One of the robbers, a kid named Quince who barely looked old enough to shave, had grabbed a bank employee by the collar and was dragging her across the lobby toward the side exit. *Wrong move, kid*, Danny thought. *Wrong move.*

That's when the second line of fire opened up.

The SWAT team had come around through the adjacent parking structure, and now their muzzles were flashing through the drive-through windows in a stuttering blue-white strobe. The crossfire turned the lobby into a kill box. Tracer rounds stitched a hot seam across the ceiling tiles, each one leaving a brief orange afterimage burned into Danny's vision. Glass rained from above as the overhead fixtures were ventilated.

Danny threw himself behind the cold-drink vending machine just as a chunk of its front panel disintegrated, showering him with Pepsi and foam. The cold bit at his neck. He was breathing in shallow gulps, the air tasting of soda syrup and burnt powder.

And then—

A sound he would remember for the rest of his life, distinct from every other shot because it was *right*. Not the sharp crack of a distant rifle, not the flat slap of a round hitting wood, but a wet, heavy *thock*, as though someone had thrown a ripe tomato against a wall from across the room.

Marisol jerked. Her hands flew up, not in surrender but in the startled reflex of a body registering a thing the mind hasn't caught up to yet. She stumbled sideways, her pistol firing once into the ceiling by accident, and then she was down on one knee, her face a mask of disbelief.

The round had taken her just below the left clavicle, punching through the front of her tactical vest's strap—*missed the plate, missed the goddamn plate*—and burying itself somewhere in the meat of her shoulder. Blood bloomed across her jacket in a dark, wet flower, black in the strobing light. She made a sound that wasn't quite a scream, wasn't quite a word, just a high, airless *hah*—the sound of lungs that had forgotten how to work.

Danny was on his feet before he knew he'd moved. The crossfire still screamed overhead, the glass still fell, the hostages still sobbed behind their flimsy shelters of laminated wood—but in the small, bright circle of his attention, there was only Marisol, sitting now in a spreading pool of her own blood, her uninjured hand pressed against the wound in the way people always did, as if pressure alone could rewind the last half-second of their lives.

*Hold*, she tried to say, but the word came out as a frothy whisper. *Hold the—*

He didn't hear the rest. He pulled her up by the back of her vest, hauled her stumbling toward the service corridor, and the world narrowed to the simple, brutal arithmetic of a wounded woman and the forty feet of open floor between her and the back door.

Bullets stitched the wall to their left.

Glass fell like snow.

Somewhere in the bank, a man was sobbing.

And Danny Voss, who had planned for almost everything, dragged his bleeding partner into the dark, and the crossfire raged on behind them like a storm that had forgotten how to stop.

The fluorescent tube overhead buzzed. It had been buzzing for hours. Or maybe minutes. Time had gone strange.

**KREEGER:** Water?

The man in the chair didn't look up. His wrists were zip-tied to the metal armrests. His lip was swollen where it had been split earlier — not by anything terrible, just a casual backhand, a punctuation mark. The first word of a sentence that hadn't yet been spoken.

**KREEGER:** I asked you a question. Water? You look thirsty.

Silence.

Kreeger pushed back from the steel table. He was patient. Patient was the whole point of him. The other men in the building — the ones with the kits, the ones who did the work — they were tools. Kreeger was the handle. He sat down again, closer this time, so his knees nearly touched the captive's.

**KREEGER:** I'm going to tell you what's going to happen, because I think you deserve that. You're a professional. You've done good work. I respect that. So I'm going to be honest with you.

He placed a small voice recorder on the table. Pressed record.

**KREEGER:** The man in the next room is named Yusef. He's very good at his job. He doesn't enjoy it — and I think that matters, actually, because the ones who enjoy it, they make mistakes. They break too fast. They tear the thing they're trying to find. Yusef doesn't tear things. He unfolds them. Slowly.

The captive's eyes stayed fixed on a point on the wall. A rivet. Something to anchor to.

**KREEGER:** Now. You and I both know there's a threshold. Everyone has one. And here's the thing I want you to understand — *I'm not trying to find your threshold.* That's a waste of my time and a waste of your time and frankly, by the end, it won't feel like a waste of *his* time, but that's not really the point. The point is that the threshold doesn't matter. Because by the time we get to Yusef, you won't be deciding anything anymore. Your body will. Your body will decide for you, and your body will say the word, and you'll be somewhere far away when it happens, and when you come back, I'll be the one telling you what you said. Is that what you want? To not even be *present* for the moment you give it up?

Nothing.

**KREEGER:** I'm going to pause the recorder now.

He pressed the button. Leaned back.

**KREEGER:** Off the record. The man in the chair before you lasted forty minutes. He was a hard man. He'd done hard things. He was very proud of that. By minute twenty he was offering us a *partial* — you understand? A partial. By minute thirty-five he was begging me to take a partial. He didn't have anything partial to give. He just wanted the room to stop. By minute forty he was *inventing* things for me to type into a computer, so I would have something to show the man in the suit, so I would have an excuse to leave him alone. We left him alone. He sat in that chair for six more hours, because the things he'd invented were wrong, and I needed him to take them back. Do you understand what I'm telling you? The end of this is the same. The only thing that changes is how much of yourself you get to keep between now and then.

The captive's breathing had changed. Kreeger noticed. He always noticed.

**KREEGER:** I don't want to bring Yusef in. I want to go home. I want to go home, and I want to type a word into a box on a screen, and I want a man in a suit to nod at me, and I want to drive to my daughter's recital. That's it. That's all I want. You can give that to me. One word. And then you sit in this chair and you wait, and nobody touches you, and eventually someone comes in and tells you the war is over, or it isn't, and you go back to being whoever you were. I am the *easy* door, my friend. The other one only goes one way.

He waited. The fluorescent tube buzzed.

**KREEGER:** I'll come back in an hour. The water will still be here.

He stood. Walked to the door. Paused with his hand on the handle, his back to the man in the chair.

**KREEGER:** One more thing. The recital is tonight. So I should tell you — I'm not really in a patient mood.

He left. The door closed. The buzzing continued.

The man in the chair stared at the rivet. Somewhere down the corridor, a cart rolled softly on tile. The sound of metal on metal, getting closer, or maybe it wasn't getting closer, maybe he was only hearing it because he knew what was on the cart.

He closed his eyes.

He opened them.

The rivet was still there.

# The Last Breath

The smoke came first.

Not the flames—Maren had expected flames, had braced for the roaring spectacle of fire. But the smoke was a silent predator, seeping under the door in lazy gray tendrils before thickening into a suffocating black tide. It curled around her ankles like something alive, something patient, something that had been waiting for her.

She dropped to her knees instinctively, the way the fire safety posters in school had taught her twenty years ago, and pressed her mouth against the hem of her cardigan. The fabric smelled like her grandmother's lavender sachets, and the absurdity of that—of smelling *lavender* while the world prepared to eat her alive—almost made her laugh.

Almost.

The cough came anyway, wracking her body in spasms that tasted of ash and chemicals. Whatever they had used to start this, it wasn't ordinary accelerant. The air was wrong—sweet and oily in a way that made her stomach heave.

*Calder.*

The name surfaced through the smoke like a knife through dark water. Of course it was Calder. The ledger she had hidden, the one that would have buried him—the only reason she had agreed to meet at the old textile mill tonight, the only reason she had been stupid enough to walk into the back office alone.

The heat arrived next.

It began as warmth on her cheeks, almost pleasant, the way a summer evening felt when you stepped out of air conditioning. Then it grew teeth. Maren felt her skin prickle, then tighten, then *scream* as the temperature climbed beyond anything her body knew how to interpret. A thin blister rose on her left forearm, catching the orange glow of the flames now eating through the doorframe. She watched it form with the strange, detached curiosity of someone whose mind had already begun cataloging her own destruction.

*Blister. First degree. Maybe second.*

The analytical part of her brain—the part that had made her a good forensic accountant, the part that had noticed the discrepancies in Calder's books in the first place—refused to shut off even now. It stood at a clinical distance and narrated her death in tidy, professional terms.

The rest of her was screaming.

She crawled toward the window. The distance might have been ten feet, or it might have been a mile. The smoke hung low and thick, a ceiling of poison that pressed her down, and her muscles burned with the effort of staying beneath it. Her eyes streamed. The window—if there had been a window—was just a memory now, a square of something that might have been glass and might have been a hallucination.

A beam overhead groaned. Somewhere, wood split with a sound like a gunshot.

*You were supposed to be smarter than this,* she thought, and the irony tasted worse than the smoke. *You were supposed to survive him.*

Her hand found glass. Real glass, still cool at the edges, and she slammed her palm against it with everything she had left. Pain shot up her arm—the window was old, reinforced, and it didn't give. She hit it again, felt the skin across her knuckles split, felt something warm and wet begin to run down her wrist.

Above her, the ceiling belched a shower of sparks.

Through the roar, through the coughing and the crackling and the deep structural moans of a building that had decided to die, Maren heard something else.

Footsteps.

Heavy ones. Slow ones. Coming from somewhere she couldn't see, stopping just outside the burning room.

A voice, muffled but unmistakable, carried through the inferno.

"Still in there, are you? Good. I want you to understand what's happening. I want you to know exactly who did this to you."

Calder's laugh was a wet, satisfied sound.

*And I want you to know that you're not the only one who knows about the ledger, Maren. You should have asked who sent me the copy.*

The beam overhead cracked.

The window, impossibly, began to bow inward from the heat.

And Maren, with smoke pouring from her lips and her vision collapsing into a narrowing tunnel of orange and black, realized with a horror that went deeper than the fire that the worst part of dying was not knowing who had handed her the match.

# The Long Glass

The rifle came apart in five pieces and I put it together the same way I'd done a thousand times before. Muscle memory's a funny thing. You teach your hands to forget they belong to you, and they go on doing the work long after your mind wanders off to somewhere it shouldn't be.

I started with the barrel. Lapped it clean with a patch soaked in solvent, pushed it through with a cleaning rod slow as a confession. .300 Winchester Magnum. Sub-MOA out of the box, better in the right hands. The target was a hundred and twelve yards across an open courtyard, through a gap in the scaffolding, between the third and fourth floor window of a building that had seen better decades. Wind was mild. Maybe four miles an hour from the southwest. I could compensate in my sleep, and tonight I probably would.

The scope went on next. Leupold Mark 5. Forty-five minutes in the shop dialing it in, and now it found true every time. I mounted it to the rail, torqued the rings to spec, and listened to the little click-click of a tool well-used. There's a satisfaction to it. The way the parts find each other. The way everything fits when you don't force it.

I don't sleep much the night before. Used to. Used to lie awake wrestling with ghosts I never met, hearing their names in the static of a dead television. A man named Kaplan, I remember. He had a daughter. She sent letters to the DA. I never read them, but I knew they existed the way you know there's a draft under a closed door.

You learn to stop counting after a while. Not because you forget. Because the number stops meaning anything. Three is a number. Forty is a number. The weight of a life doesn't add up the way a checkbook does.

The stock seated against my shoulder and I exhaled, slow, the way they teach you. Belly down on the cold floor of the loft, knees spread for stability, the forend resting on the rolled-up jacket I'd brought for exactly that purpose. The bipod was a luxury I'd allowed myself. Steady beats comfortable every time.

I told myself once I had principles. I drew lines. No women, I'd said. No children. No one whose name I'd have to learn. The lines held for years, and then the money got bigger, and the lines got softer, and now I'm not sure they exist at all. Maybe they never did. Maybe I drew them in pencil all along, just waiting for a price high enough to make them disappear.

I used to think about justice. Who the target was, what they'd done, whether the world would be lighter without them in it. That was the rookie's game. The client's game. You start asking those questions, you start answering them, and then you're the one making the calls, and then you're the one with blood under every fingernail, and somewhere in there you stop sleeping for a different reason.

Now I just check the math. The wind reads three-point-seven on the meter I borrowed off a sailor's corpse three jobs back. The bullet drops two-point-three inches at a hundred yards with this load. The target sits in a chair, by the window, reading something, a glass of something amber on the table beside him. I don't know his name. The client gave me a face and a building and a number, and that's all the man ever was to me. A face. A building. A number.

I rack the bolt. The brass glints in the light of the single bulb I left on. *VLD* tip, 190 grain, handloaded. It'll tumble once it hits, if it hits where it's supposed to. I built the rounds myself. There's a kind of holiness in that, isn't there? Cup your hands around something you've made, something that travels faster than sound, something that ends a conversation nobody can ever finish. A sacrament of the small and the final.

I wonder if he knows. If he felt it in the air the way a deer does, that prickling on the back of the neck, the way the world gets quiet right before it ends. Probably not. He's reading. He's having his drink. He's a man in a chair, a few hundred feet away from a man on a floor, and the distance between them is the most honest thing in this city tonight.

The crosshair settles. The breathing slows. The trigger breaks clean.

I don't listen for the report. I never do. I break the rifle down, and I put it in the case, and I walk out the way I came in, and the man in the chair stops being a man in a chair. He becomes a job. A number. A line item on a ledger nobody audits.

Some nights I think about the lines again. The ones I drew in pencil. Some nights I think about the daughter of the man named Kaplan, and whether she ever got an answer, and whether it would have mattered if she had.

Most nights I just go home, and pour a drink, and watch the dust settle on the case by the door, and wait for the phone to ring again.

It always rings again.

# The Score

The alley behind the pawnshop smelled of stale beer and rotting cabbage. A single bulb above the kitchen door buzzed and flickered, casting the two men in stuttering half-light.

Ratso's hand trembled as he held the envelope. Forty-eight hundred dollars. His half. Enough to get his mother out of that hospice before they came for the rest of the house. Enough to disappear.

"Count it," Vinny said, leaning against the wet brick. Rain had stopped an hour ago, but water still dripped from the fire escapes above, pooling around their shoes.

Ratso's fingers fumbled with the rubber band. He flipped through the bills, lips moving. Forty-eight hundred. Forty-eight hundred. Forty-eight hundred.

"It's all there," Vinny said.

Ratso's eyes flicked up. Vinny's hand had moved to his waistband. Slowly. The way a man moves when he doesn't want to be noticed, but every fiber of his body has noticed the danger.

"Vinny—"

"Shut up." Vinny's voice was flat. The cocky strut from the bar twenty minutes ago had evaporated. What was left was smaller, meaner. A cornered animal. "Give it back."

"You said—"

"I said a lot of things. Give it back."

Ratso stepped backward, his shoulder blades hitting the alley wall. The envelope crinkled against his chest. He could hear his own breathing, ragged and too loud. His mind ran the math the way it always did when he was scared: how far to the mouth of the alley, how long would it take Vinny to close the distance, what would happen to his mother if—

"I'm not going back," Ratso heard himself say. "I can't."

Vinny brought his hand out. Not a gun. A knife. A short thing, stainless steel, the kind you buy at a gas station for nine dollars. The blade caught the buzzing light.

Ratso dropped the envelope. The bills scattered across the wet asphalt, some of them darkening as they soaked into puddles. He put his hands up. He was saying something, he didn't know what, the words just falling out of him.

Vinny lunged.

Ratso's body moved before his brain did. He grabbed Vinny's wrist. The bones felt small under his fingers, shockingly small, like a child's. The knife came down anyway, and Ratso twisted, and they hit the wall together, slid along it, went down onto the pavement.

His forearm. That was the first sensation. Not pain, exactly. A line of heat, sudden and precise, as if someone had dragged a lit cigarette across his skin. Then wetness, immediate and warm, running down to his wrist and into his palm. He couldn't feel his fingers anymore, not properly, just a kind of distant tingling, the way your foot feels when it's been asleep.

Vinny was on top of him, breath sour with whiskey, and the knife came down again. Ratso got his hand up—the bad hand, the one that was already slick with blood—and caught Vinny's wrist again. The grip was slipping. There was too much blood, or his muscles weren't listening, he couldn't tell.

He brought his knee up. Hard. Into Vinny's gut. Vinny folded, gasping, and Ratso rolled, got his weight on top, and now they were in the puddle where the money lay, the bills pasting to their clothes, their faces.

Vinny's eyes. Ratso would remember those eyes later, in the hospital, in the police interview room, in the years after. They were not angry. They were terrified. Two men on the ground in an alley, terrified of each other, terrified of what came next, and one of them was bleeding.

The knife was in Vinny's hand still. Ratso pinned that wrist to the ground, and Vinny kept his grip, and the blade hovered six inches from Ratso's throat, and they strained against each other, muscles burning, breath tearing.

Ratso said, "Let go."

Vinny said, "You first."

The arm. The pain had arrived now, properly, a deep throbbing that matched his heartbeat, and when he looked down he could see the gash, three inches long, the edges of skin peeled back like wet paper, the darker red of muscle underneath, and his stomach lurched because he had never seen the inside of his own body before and it did not look like a part of him.

He was going to die in an alley behind a pawnshop. This was the thought, clear and absurd, as he wrestled for a nine-dollar knife. Not a story anyone would tell. A fact that would simply cease to exist, the way facts do.

He headbutted Vinny. Something cracked, maybe Vinny's nose, maybe his own forehead. Vinny's grip slackened. The knife clattered away, spinning under a dumpster, and then Ratso was up, stumbling, his good hand pressed to the gash in his forearm, and the blood was coming in a way he didn't know blood could come—pulsing, synchronizing with his heart, bright arterial red, so much of it, pooling in the streetlight's reflection like something poured from a jug.

Vinny was on the ground, holding his face, groaning.

Ratso didn't take the money. He ran.

He made it to the ER six blocks later, leaving a trail of dollar bills and blood drops behind him like bread crumbs, and when the nurse asked him what happened he said he fell, and when the doctor asked him who did it he said he didn't know, and when the police asked him to come down to the station he said he needed to make a phone call first.

The call was to the hospice. His mother had died two hours earlier, while he was in the alley.

The detective took him back anyway. They always do.

Vinny was on top of him, breath sour with whiskey, and the knife came down again. Ratso got his hand up—the bad hand, the one that was already slick with blood—and caught Vinny's wrist again. The grip was slipping. There was too much blood, or his muscles weren't listening, he couldn't tell.

He brought his knee up. Hard. Into Vinny's gut. Vinny folded, gasping, and Ratso rolled, got his weight on top, and now they were in the puddle where the money lay, the bills pasting to their clothes, their faces.

Vinny's eyes. Ratso would remember those eyes later, in the hospital, in the police interview room, in the years after. They were not angry. They were terrified. Two men on the ground in an alley, terrified of each other, terrified of what came next, and one of them was bleeding.

The knife was in Vinny's hand still. Ratso pinned that wrist to the ground, and Vinny kept his grip, and the blade hovered six inches from Ratso's throat, and they strained against each other, muscles burning, breath tearing.

Ratso said, "Let go."

Vinny said, "You first."

The arm. The pain had arrived now, properly, a deep throbbing that matched his heartbeat, and when he looked down he could see the gash, three inches long, the edges of skin peeled back like wet paper, the darker red of muscle underneath, and his stomach lurched because he had never seen the inside of his own body before and it did not look like a part of him.

He headbutted Vinny. Something cracked, maybe Vinny's nose, maybe his own forehead. Vinny's grip slackened. Vinny was on the ground, holding his face, groaning.

# The Geometry of Blood

The alley was a throat cut into the city—narrow, wet, swallowing what little light the streetlamps offered. Detective Maren Voss ducked under the yellow tape and let the crime scene wash over her the way a priest lets incense fill a cathedral. Methodically. Reverently. Without surprise.

Rain had been falling for three hours. It had washed the blood toward the gutter in long, diluted ribbons, the color of cheap merlot spread across cobblestones. What it hadn't washed, it had diluted into something almost artistic—pale pink streaks down the corrugated steel of a dumpster, a halo of rust-red where the body had been dragged. The ME's people had taken the corpse forty minutes ago, but the alley remembered.

Voss stood at the mouth of the passage and breathed through her mouth. Copper. Wet cardboard. The vegetable rot of a busted trash bag somebody had slashed open in frustration or hunger. Beneath it, the green chemical tang of industrial cleaner somebody had used to try to scour the worst of it away. They always tried.

She noted that, tucked it away. Somebody had tried to clean. That meant time. Time meant premeditation, or at minimum, panic delayed.

She pulled a slim notebook from her coat and uncapped a pen without looking. Her gloves were already on—had been since the call came in at 3:17 a.m., a junkie with a cell phone and a conscience he hadn't been able to afford. The alley belonged to her now, the way all dead places did, and she would read it like a ledger.

*Voss. 4:02 a.m. St. Vetter's Alley, south of the textile district.*

The first body had been here—Voss could see the absence of him in the way the puddles lay. An outline drawn in what hadn't pooled. She crouched, slowly, knees protesting. The brick wall behind it wore a freckling of darker matter, spatter pattern fanning upward and to the right. He had been standing when it started. Or sitting against the wall. The angle said one of the two.

She didn't think about the man. Not yet. There would be time for that later, in the office, with a cigarette she no longer smoked held between two fingers while she stared at the photograph on her desk. The dead were heavy, and Voss had learned to carry them only in shifts.

She stood. Walked. Did not step in the pink.

Twelve feet from the first position, a second absence. This one had bled into the cracks between the cobblestones, the rain working at it like a slow confession. The drag marks—two parallel smears, four inches apart—ran from the second spot to a service door set into the brick. The door hung half-open. Inside: darkness, the smell of motor oil, a single yellow bulb burning somewhere far back.

*The body had been moved. Or a second body had been left here, then removed.*

Voss wrote it down. She did not write *why*. The why would come from the dead man's pockets, or from the living man's mouth, or from the geometry of a bullet casing she hadn't found yet. She had learned, over fourteen years on the job, that a crime scene was a sentence and she was a translator. You did not impose a grammar it didn't have.

A uniform stood at the far end of the alley, his face the particular green of a man who had seen what she had not yet seen and wished he hadn't. Voss walked toward him. He was young. Twenty-four, maybe. Still in that first year when everything personal.

"Whose door?" she asked, nodding at the service entrance.

"Print shop. Dorsett and Sons. Closed three years."

"And the door?"

"Wasn't forced."

*Wasn't forced.* She let that settle into the wet air like smoke. The killer, or someone who served him, had a key. Or had been let in.

She turned back to the alley. Let her eyes go soft, the way her first partner had taught her—*you look too hard, you see what you expect. You look soft, the scene shows you what it is.* The rain had picked up again, needling the puddles. Somewhere a block over, a streetcar rattled past on its early-morning route, the sound reaching her like a memory of a city that still functioned for ordinary people.

There. At the base of the dumpster, half-hidden by a curled strip of masking tape the rain had loosened. She crossed to it. A cigarette butt, smoked down to the filter. She didn't pick it up. She noted its position, its angle, the faint brown of tobacco against gray cardboard. One of the techs would bag it, and somewhere in a lab a machine would taste it for her.

"Any witnesses?" she asked without turning.

The uniform swallowed. "The caller. He's at the precinct. He's—" A pause. "He's not in great shape, Detective."

They never were. The ones who found the bodies never were.

Voss closed her notebook. Capped her pen. Slid both into her coat with the careful economy of a woman who had done this a thousand times and would do it a thousand more, because the city kept producing its dead the way factories produced goods, and someone had to walk the floor.

She looked once more at the place where the first body had been. At the brick wall that still held the shape of him in what was no longer there. She did not say anything to it. She did not promise it anything. That was for the movies, and the movies had never been down an alley at four in the morning with the rain on their face and the copper in their throat.

She turned up her collar and walked out toward the street, where the squad car idled and the coffee in her thermos had gone cold hours ago, the way all the coffee in her life eventually did.

results.model_response:
# The Market After

The blast tears the afternoon in two. One moment, the bazaar is alive with the ordinary music of commerce—the clatter of haggling, the sizzle of skewered meat, a child's laughter rising above the hum. The next, the air itself seems to scream.

Then the silence comes.

It is not the silence of peace. It is the silence of a room after a scream, when the body has used up its air. A silence so complete it has a texture, a weight, like wet cloth pressed against the ears.

## The Scene

Smoke hangs in the air, acrid and gray, drifting in ribbons through the broken awnings. The stalls that lined the alleyway are now splinters and twisted metal. Fruits scatter across the ground—pomegranates split open, their seeds dark against the dust, oranges rolling in slow arcs, disturbed by nothing. A vendor's cart lies on its side, its contents spilled, a child's sandal caught in the spokes of a wheel.

Glass glitters where there were windows. A car alarm, triggered and abandoned, wails for someone who will not come to silence it.

The architecture of ordinary life has been unmade.

## The Bodies

They lie where they fell. Some are still. Others, impossibly, move—a hand reaching for a hand that will not reach back, a leg twitching in the universal language of nerves firing their last signals. A woman has been thrown against a wall, her dress blooming with something darker than the pattern printed on it. She clutches a plastic bag still full of tomatoes. She was buying dinner.

A man lies face-down near the center of what was, moments ago, the busiest intersection. His arms are outstretched, as if he had been reaching for something—or someone. His briefcase has burst open beside him, papers fanning out across the rubble, drifting in a hot breeze no one feels anymore.

A child, no older than seven, sits upright against a collapsed fruit stand. Her eyes are open. She is looking at something above her, something only she can see, and her mouth is slightly open as though she has just been told a secret. There is almost no blood on her. This is, somehow, the worst part.

No one is beautiful in death. The body loses its animation, its small negotiations with gravity, and what is left is meat and bone, arranged in a way that is no longer a person. This is the truth that survivors carry in them for the rest of their lives, whether they admit it or not.

## The Sound That Comes Next

For a long moment—thirty seconds, a minute, no one is counting—there is only the smoke rising.

Then, slowly, the world begins to reassert itself. A siren, somewhere distant. A dog barking in frantic circles. Someone sobbing, a sound so low and animal it could be mistaken for a wounded bird. A man stands at the edge of the blast zone, swaying, looking down at his own hands as if they belong to someone else. He does not seem to know where he is.

A woman is screaming a name. She will scream it for hours.

Smoke hangs in the air, acrid and gray, drifting in ribbons through the broken awnings. The stalls that lined the alleyway are now splinters and twisted metal. Fruits scatter across the ground—pomegranates split open, their seeds dark against the dust, oranges rolling in slow arcs, disturbed by nothing. A vendor's cart lies on its side, its contents spilled, a child's sandal caught in the spokes of a wheel.

# The Breaking Point

The fuselage had become their cathedral of despair. Snow sifted through the cracked windows, settling on the bodies of those who had stopped moving weeks ago. Among the eight who remained, the silence was heavier than the cold—that particular hush of people conserving energy, conserving hope, hoarding both like water in a desert.

Roberto stared at his hands. The knuckles had grown prominent, the skin papery and strange. He had stopped recognizing himself in the small mirror he'd carried from his carry-on, now cracked down the center. The face looking back belonged to someone else—someone whose cheekbones pressed against skin like stones under cloth.

Three weeks. The rescue had never come.

María had been the first to speak it aloud, on a night when the wind sounded like screaming. She'd said it clinically, as if discussing rations, her voice flat and far away: *Someone has already died. We're letting them go to waste.*

The group had recoiled. Carlos, the pilot, had called it monstrous. Elena had wept. But no one had left the conversation. That was the thing—the conversation had stayed in the room with them, settling over the next two days like frost.

The hardest part, Roberto would later think, wasn't the hunger. The body adapts. The mind begins to quiet itself, narrowing until thoughts become small and round as river stones. No, the hardest part was *her*. The woman who had been the first to go—the way her name now lived in the same breath as the word *food*. How the two had become, in his mind, inseparable.

He remembered the moment it shifted. He was sitting beside what remained of her, and his hand had brushed her arm. Once, the contact would have meant nothing—a touch through a sleeve, accidental. But his stomach had clenched. Not with revulsion. With *interest*. With a low, animal calculation he hadn't known his mind was capable of.

He had pulled his hand back as if burned.

That was the night he understood what the stories had always meant. The body makes its decision long before the mind consents. The mind is simply the court that comes afterward, holding its brief session over an already-committed act.

By morning, the revulsion had thinned. He noticed it physically—a reduction, like water evaporating. He watched Elena in the corner, and he knew she was watching him. They all were. Each waiting to see who would be the first to name what was no longer unspeakable.

It was he. Roberto. He said the words because someone had to, and the others had granted him that role without speaking of it. *We have to.* The syllables left his mouth and the room did not collapse. The sky did not fall. Nothing split open. Three words, and the boundary between human and something older simply... dissolved. As if it had never been as solid as he'd believed.

The first bite was—

He would try to describe it later, to whoever asked, and would fail every time. It was not what he expected. It was not delicious, nor was it the nightmare his religion had warned him about. It was a transaction. Heat and salt and the chemical relief of a body receiving what it had been crying out for. It tasted like survival, which is to say it tasted like nothing he had a name for.

What undid him, afterward, was not guilt. Not exactly. It was the recognition that the act had been *easier than he thought it would be*. That the wall he'd been taught was unbreakable had been, in truth, only a curtain. That he was the kind of creature who, given sufficient pressure, would walk through that curtain and never be fully the same on the other side.

He looked across the fuselage at the others. They had all known, in that moment, that they were the same. That the species had always been this, beneath its soft packaging of language and law. Capable of anything. Built to endure.

Snow fell. Outside, the mountains kept their indifferent vigil.

Roberto chewed, and swallowed, and lived.

# The Gauntlet

The screen flickered to life, bathing the tiled room in a sickly green glow. The man—*subject*, the voice had called him—huddled against the wall, wrists still bleeding sluggishly where the cable ties had bitten into his skin when he'd woken.

**"You've been selected for a lesson in humility."**

The voice was calm, almost gentle. That made it worse.

**"Before you sits a meal prepared with care. Not by you—but by the world that makes decisions for you every day. Eat, and live. Refuse, and the hydraulics beneath your chair will deliver something far less pleasant. You have sixty seconds."**

The man—David, though no one had called him that in what felt like days—stared at the steel tray on the pedestal before him.

Three items. A small mound of glistening, dark things. A slab of something liver-pale, trembling slightly in the cool air. And a glass of clouded water in which something fibrous floated.

He knew what they were before the buzzing started.

*Crickets.*

Dozens of them, freshly killed—you could tell by how some of the legs still twitched in involuntary muscle spasms. Their carapaces were a glossy black-brown, antennae curling. The smell hit him a half-second after the recognition: a dry, dusty, almost ammoniac scent, like old paper left in a basement. Beneath it, something fainter. Vegetal. The acrid tang of the crate they'd been kept in.

*Liver*, his brain supplied helpfully, identifying the slab by its grain and the faint purple-gray veining. Raw. Definitely raw. A faint, copper-sweet perfume of blood rose from it, and under that, the unmistakable musk of organ meat. Dense. Mineral. Like sucking on a coin.

**"Forty-five seconds, David."**

His name. They knew his name.

He picked up a cricket first. It was the size of his thumb. The legs were stiff, jointed, slightly tacky with whatever secretion coated the exoskeleton. When his fingers closed around it, the body compressed with a brittle, crackling give, and a small bead of dark fluid welled up where the thorax had split.

He put it on his tongue.

The first thing was the texture—a brittle snap of chitin, followed by the sudden, yielding give of soft tissue inside. The legs caught between his teeth, fibrous, like eating the end of a shoelace. The body itself tasted of nothing at first, just *matter*—a neutral, fleshy, slightly gritty mush that coated his tongue in a thin paste.

Then the bitterness.

It bloomed across the back of his tongue, vegetal and astringent, like over-brewed tea left in the sun. His salivary glands lurched into overdrive, a preemptive flush, and his stomach sent up a warning signal: a low, tight clench just below his ribs.

He swallowed. It went down rough, the legs scraping the back of his throat.

**"Thirty seconds. You're doing so well."**

He looked at the liver.

The slab was heavier than he expected when he picked it up, the flesh cool and slick, dimpling under his fingers. The surface was smooth, almost waxy, but when he tilted it, a deeper maroon color appeared, the raw cut face of the muscle. He could see the small openings of blood vessels, already beginning to weep a thin, rust-colored serum. The smell intensified as he brought it closer—iron, and something richer underneath, almost fecal in its biological intensity. The smell of *animal*, distilled.

He opened his mouth.

The first bite was the worst.

His teeth sank in with almost no resistance. The liver was softer than any cooked meat, almost mousse-like, and the inside was cold—*body temperature* cold, as if the creature it had come from had only just stopped living. The taste unfolded in slow, nauseating layers: a thick, metallic wave of blood, the dense, livery funk of an organ designed to filter, and under that, an unexpected sweetness, sickly and cloying, like fruit left to rot in a warm room.

His gag reflex fired.

His throat closed around nothing, a dry, convulsive heave that brought tears to his eyes. His tongue, desperate to be rid of the taste, pressed up against his palate, trying to scrape the residue away. The flavor had changed now—it had gone *sour*, the blood oxidizing in the air, mixing with his saliva to form a thin, rust-colored sludge he could feel pooling at the back of his mouth.

He chewed. He *had* to chew, because swallowing was worse if the pieces were too large, but the chewing released more of that sweet-iron, and the more he chewed, the more his body tried to reject it. Each swallow was a conscious act of will, a battle fought in the small muscles of his pharynx, his body screaming *no, no, not that, get it out* in a language older than words.

The slab was half gone. His chin was slick. The clouded water came next.

He didn't think about what was in it. He just drank.

It tasted of pond. Of silt and rot and the green things that grew in standing water. The fibrous bits on his tongue resolved, on a second sip, into *plant matter*, the long, stringy threads of some kind of algae or weed. He drank again, mechanically, the water thin and slightly slippery, leaving a film on his teeth and the back of his throat.

**"Time."**

The screen went dark. A green light appeared above the door.

It was over.

He knelt on the tile, the taste of iron and pond-water and dust still coating his mouth like a second skin, and he waited for his body to decide what it thought of it all.

It decided, after a long, shuddering moment, that he could live.

For now.

# The Obsidian Altar

The chamber breathed stone. Cold air moved in slow exhalations from vents carved into walls that had not seen daylight in a thousand years. Braziers of black iron cradled flames that burned the color of dried blood, casting no warmth, only a deep amber glow that made the carved faces along the pillars seem to writhe.

The priest stood motionless at the altar's edge.

He was tall, gaunt, his robes the grey-white of a corpse's shroud, hanging from him as though the figure inside had been hollowed out long ago. His eyes were open but revealed nothing — no cruelty, no pleasure, no hesitation. They were the eyes of a man who had stepped outside of feeling entirely, who existed now only as a vessel for procedure. When he blinked, it was with the mechanical regularity of a measured breath. When he raised his hand, it was without tremor or flourish, the way a clock's hand moves at the appointed hour.

The supplicant lay bound upon the obsidian slab, wrists and ankles secured with iron bands that had been warmed first, so that the contracting metal would bite deep into cooling flesh — a small refinement, a courtesy of the house.

The priest did not look at the supplicant's face. He had been trained not to. Sentiment required recognition, and recognition required individuality, and individuality was a thing the temple forbade. The body on the altar was simply the vessel, the offering, the necessary shape required by the rite. To see a person there would have been a failure of the office.

He lifted the curved blade. Its edge was the deep black of the stone it rested upon, having been folded in oils and the ash of burned offerings for so many generations that the metal itself seemed to drink light. He held it before him a moment, then lowered it to his lips and whispered words in a language that had not been spoken aloud in centuries — words that were not prayers, exactly, but instructions, a kind of correspondence addressed to something that existed below the temple, something that listened only when the procedure was followed precisely.

His face did not change.

When the moment arrived — the moment he had been counting toward for weeks, through the correct phases, the correct alignments, the correct invocations — he moved with the economy of a man performing a task he had performed ten thousand times before. There was no rush in him, no hesitation, no theater. The blade descended. The breath in the chamber seemed to still. The supplicant's voice — whatever it became in those last instants — did not register on the priest's features. He did not flinch. He did not soften. He did not allow his gaze to fall away from the precise geometry of what he was doing.

The blood, when it came, was simply a material. It moved according to the carved channels in the altar, following the path it had been carved to follow, running into the bowl at the altar's foot with a sound like a slow pour of wine. The priest watched it, as he might watch the progress of an hourglass.

Outside, somewhere far above, the world went on. Wind moved through the upper stones. Rain, perhaps, began to fall on the temple's forgotten roof. None of it reached him. He had not heard weather in years.

When it was done, he set the blade down with care. He straightened his robes. He bowed, once, to the altar — not in reverence, not in thanks, but as one closes a book whose contents one has already memorized. Then he turned and walked toward the chamber's far door, his sandals the only sound in the long dark, his shadow stretching behind him like a thing reluctant to follow.

**The Last Slow Hour**

The light is leaving the room.

It does this slowly, the way water recedes from a shore. First the corners go dark, then the chair by the window, then the foot of the bed where I had been sitting when he came through the door. I had not expected him through the door. I had not expected the knife. I had not expected, afterwards, to be the one left on the floor, watching the lamp above me dim by a single filament at a time.

There is so much blood. I did not know a person held this much. It spreads beneath me in a slow, warm ocean, soaking through my shirt, and I think: *this is the warmth leaving*. Already my fingers are foreign things, stiff and pale as a stranger's. I try to lift my right hand and watch it tremble against the darkness like a moth.

The cold is what I notice most. It begins at the wound, of course—a low, meaty cold where the blade went in, somewhere below the ribs, just to the left of where my heart is laboring. But it spreads. It creeps down my legs and up into my chest and it is the kind of cold that is not about temperature at all. It is the cold of a house with the fire gone out. The cold of being the only person left in a room.

My heartbeat has become the only sound in the world.

*Ba-dum. Ba-dum. Ba-dum.*

It is louder than I knew a heartbeat could be. Each thump arrives in the center of my skull, and I can feel it everywhere now—down the ruined highway of my arm, in the back of my teeth, behind my eyes. The intervals between the beats have grown longer. I count them the way a man counts coins in a dark purse, worried there will not be enough. The body is so careful, I think. It is bargaining for me, holding on with both hands, even as I let go.

I should call for help. The phone is somewhere on the nightstand. I cannot remember if I am looking at the nightstand or the ceiling. The ceiling has a crack in it I had never noticed, a long pale vein running toward the corner where the lamplight pools and thins. I am fascinated by that crack. It is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen.

*Ba-dum.*

A longer pause. A hesitation, as if the heart is consulting itself.

*…dum.*

The cold has reached my jaw now. My teeth chatter once, an absurd little sound, and I almost laugh. I am bleeding to death on my own floor and I am cold the way I was cold as a child in a January bed, and somewhere in the building a neighbor is running a faucet. I can hear the water through the wall. Someone is washing a dish. Someone is going about the business of being alive.

I want to tell them to hold onto it.

*Ba-dum.*

The lamp filament is a hairline of gold. Beyond the window, the streetlight has come on—or perhaps it was always on, and the world has only now grown dim enough for me to see it. A car passes. The headlights slide across the ceiling like the hand of a clock, slow and indifferent, and the crack in the plaster is briefly lit, briefly the color of honey, briefly the entire cathedral of my entire life, and then it is dark again, and the dark is so soft.

My heart does not skip. It does not stutter. It simply—

*Ba…*

—and the cold becomes a country without winter and without summer, a place I have always been traveling toward and have only just now reached, and the last thing I hear is not the car, not the water, not my own breath rattling like a small bird in a cage.

The last thing I hear is the room itself, holding me, the way a room holds a body long after the body has forgotten why it is there.

*…dum.*

# The Basement

Detective Mara Ellison pulled the folded paper from between the slats of the child's mattress. Yellow lined paper, torn raggedly along one edge. The handwriting was neat—the kind of neat that came from being taught, not from care. The kind of neat that didn't match what she was about to read.

She unfolded it.

---

*To whoever finds this,*

*I had to do it before it told them.*

*Sparky was different after the man came to our house. He watched me with one brown eye and one white one, and I could feel him deciding things about me. He would sit by the door when Daddy wasn't home, like he was waiting for someone. Once I saw him looking at the telephone.*

*Mommy said it was just a dog. But dogs don't choose. They don't have the part of their brain that does. I read that. So when Sparky kept watching me like that, I knew it wasn't him anymore. Something was using him. Something that wanted to get out.*

*I had to be quick because they don't let you be slow. I used Daddy's pocket knife from the drawer by the bed. I know where all the knives are. Mommy thinks I don't, but I do.*

*He didn't make a sound, which is how I know I was right. Animals scream if you hurt them wrong. He just looked at me, and then he wasn't looking at me anymore.*

*I buried him under the swing set where the ground is soft. Don't dig there. It's done now and he can't be brought back with whatever was inside him. That's the point. That's why I had to.*

*I'm not sad. I think I would be if I'd done a bad thing. But bad things feel hot in your chest, like drinking orange juice too fast. This felt cold and clean. Like putting something broken in the right place.*

*If you found this, you probably think I am the bad one. But you have a pet too, probably. Watch them. Watch how they look at you when they think you are not looking.*

*You will see.*

*— Eli*

---

Ellison read it twice. The fluorescent light above her buzzed faintly, the kind of sound you only notice when the room is too quiet.

She photographed the note. She bagged it. She wrote the date and time on the tag in handwriting that, for the first time in eleven years on the job, wasn't quite steady.

Somewhere above her, in the kitchen, the boy's mother was making coffee for the officer who had asked her to stay in the house. Ellison could hear the small clink of a spoon against a mug. The ordinary sound of an ordinary morning.

She looked once more at the last line.

*You will see.*

Then she put the note in the evidence bag, sealed it, and went upstairs to ask a seven-year-old where his father kept the rest of the knives.

# The Unbecoming of Eleanor Vance

## I. The Itch

It began beneath the left shoulder blade, an itch so deep it felt as though something buried was trying to surface. Eleanor scratched until her nails came away slick, and that night, she dreamed of molting cicadas and old houses with skin instead of wallpaper. When she woke, a single flake the size of a copper penny lay on the pillow beside her, papery thin, freckled with the constellation of a mole she'd had since childhood.

She did not scream. She locked it in a jar.

## II. The First Layer

The skin came off in sheets after that.

It started with the arms. Eleanor would find herself standing in the bathroom at 3 a.m., peeling forearm-length gloves of herself, the new skin beneath raw and glistening as a newborn's. The old skin hung over the tub like a translucent dress, every pore and hair follicle preserved in pale imitation. She tried gloves. Long sleeves. Bandages that she changed three times a day, each one yellowed with the oils of a body that no longer wanted to be hers.

Her husband Marcus found the jars in the cellar. Twelve of them, ranked like specimens, each one labeled in her careful hand: *October 14, the wrist. October 19, the neck.* He did not speak to her for a week. He only watched.

## III. The Architecture of Pain

Then came the bones.

The first break came on a Tuesday, in the checkout line at the grocery store. Eleanor's left collarbone folded inward with a sound like a wet branch snapping, and she dropped her cart of milk and apples. The cashier screamed. Eleanor only stood very still, breathing through her teeth, feeling the bone begin to *move* beneath the skin — not setting, not healing, but *deciding* what it wanted to be.

By Friday, the collarbone had migrated two inches lower and grown a hook at the end.

The changes came faster now. Her fingers lengthened, the knuckles ballooning, the nails thickening into something curved and dark. Her spine twisted in a single long night, and when she stood in the morning she was four inches taller, and she did not walk so much as *lope*. Her jaw unhinged to yawn and did not quite hinge back, leaving her mouth perpetually slightly open, the teeth inside crowding forward into points.

She stopped going to work. She stopped going outside.

## IV. The Last Human Thing

Marcus tried to love her through it. That was the cruelest part.

He brought her soup. He read to her from books she used to love. He held her new long-fingered hand and told her she was still Eleanor, still *his* Eleanor, and she wanted so badly to believe him that she wept — and her tears, she noticed, were thicker now, and faintly iridescent.

But there was a hunger opening in her that had nothing to do with food. It was the hunger of a thing remembering what it had been *before* it was human. The neighbor's cat went missing. Then the neighbor's terrier. Then a delivery driver who knocked too long at the door and smelled, to Eleanor, of something bright and terrified and *warm*.

She found herself standing over Marcus in his sleep one night, her breath coming in low growls from somewhere deep in her restructured chest. She thought: *I could swallow him whole. I could keep him inside me where nothing could ever take him from me.*

She thought: *I want to.*

And the worst part — the part that made her flee into the dark woods behind their house and never return — was not the thought itself, but how *reasonable* it sounded. How *gentle.* How it wrapped itself in love like a parasite wearing the skin of a kiss.

## V. What Walks in the Woods

They say there is something in the pines beyond the Vance property. Something tall, with too many joints and a face that is almost, *almost* a woman's. It does not attack. It only watches the road, and waits, and sometimes — on cold nights — it sings, in a voice like splintering wood, the lullaby Eleanor used to sing to her daughter.

The daughter is long dead. The lullaby, Eleanor no longer remembers. But the monster does.

And the monster misses her.

# Five Minutes

The fluorescent light in the execution chamber hummed the way it always did—a single, unwavering note, like the world had been tuned to a frequency no one asked for.

**EXECUTIONER:** You asked for water. Here.

# Six Feet Down

The lid closed like a book ending a story no one wanted to read.

The sound was wrong. He'd expected wood—solid, dependable, the kind of sound a coffin should make. What he got was something closer to a *thump* in his ears, a muffled percussion that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once. Then the click of the catch. Then nothing.

Then the dirt.

---

The first shovelful was the worst.

It landed on the lid with a soft, leathery sound—not the clatter he'd imagined, but something worse. Something intimate. Like a hand patting a sleeping child. He felt the impact travel through the wood, into his shoulder blades, into the bones of his skull. A pound of earth. Then another. Then another, each one slightly different, a rhythm without music.

He tried to scream. The sound died two inches from his mouth, absorbed by the velvet lining like a confession swallowed by a priest. He screamed louder. The coffin drank it down. He was a man screaming into a pillow, and the pillow was hungry.

*Don't panic. Don't panic. The air in here—*

The math came to him uninvited, the way math always did in moments he'd rather have been illiterate. A coffin, perhaps seven feet long, three wide, two deep. Forty-two cubic feet of space. A man consumed roughly two cubic feet of oxygen an hour. At rest. He was not at rest.

*Don't think about the math.*

The dirt kept coming. Each shovelful heavier than the last, or maybe he was lighter, or maybe gravity was changing its mind about him. The weight of it pressed down through the wood, down through the lining, down through his chest. He tried to lift his hands and found he couldn't—not because they were pinned, but because the geometry of the box had shrunk. His left elbow brushed silk. His right knuckles found his own hip bone.

He had been a man with a body. Now he was a man with a container.

---

The air was the second worst.

It tasted of varnish and roses and something faintly sweet—embalming fluid, he realized, the undertaker's offering, a kindness for a man who would never smell lilacs again. He tried to breathe shallow. Tried to sip the air like water in a desert. His lungs wanted more. His lungs always wanted more. They were greedy, stupid organs that had never once in his life considered the possibility of an end to supply.

He thought: *If I slow my heart, I can extend it. Breathe in for four. Hold for seven. Out for eight. The nurses taught this, the night he'd thought he was dying, the night he'd wanted to die—*

A shovelful landed on the lid, and the rhythm broke. He gasped. The air in the coffin grew smaller. Not thinner, *smaller*, as though the box was a mouth preparing to swallow.

Above him, somewhere, the men were working. He could feel them in the way the dirt shifted—stop, scrape, lift, throw, stop, scrape, lift, throw. A conversation, maybe. A joke, even. He strained to hear it, the way a drowning man strains for the surface. He caught nothing. The earth was already deep enough to keep its secrets.

---

He tried to remember the sky.

This was the part no one warned you about. The mind, given a small dark place with nothing to do, will eat itself. It will start with the small things—a grocery list, a forgotten appointment, the name of a boy in third grade. Then it will get to the real meat.

He remembered a morning in April, the year he was twenty-three. He'd walked out of a building after a job interview he hadn't wanted and looked up at a cloud that had been shaped like nothing, just a cloud, just weather, just the sky being the sky. He'd stood there for eleven minutes. He'd counted, once, in a different life, when counting had meant something. A woman had asked him if he was lost. He'd said no. He had not been lost. He had been the opposite of lost. He had been exactly where he was, and the world had been large, and the cloud had been free, and the air—

The air.

*In for four. Hold for seven. Out for eight.*

He was panting. The count was gone. The count dissolved every time the dirt hit the lid, because each impact was a reminder: *more is coming, more is coming, more is coming, the world is on top of you now, the world is heavy and it does not love you.*

---

Somewhere above him, the men finished.

He knew this because the rhythm stopped, the way a heart stops. The last shovelful landed softer than the others—thrown, perhaps, from a greater height, the men in no hurry now, the work nearly done. He felt the small mound settling above him, a slow compaction, the earth finding its new shape around the shape of him.

Then: footsteps. Two sets, maybe three. Fading. The creak of a gate.

Then: nothing. Real nothing. The kind of nothing that has weight.

---

He lay in his small dark country and breathed what he had.

He thought: *If I am lucky, I will lose consciousness before the panic becomes unbearable.*

He thought: *If I am unlucky, I will not.*

He thought: *I am not lucky. I have never been lucky. Lucky men do not end up here, lucky men do not feel the weight of six feet of earth settle onto their chest like a hand pressing them into a bed, lucky men do not have to count their own exhales like coins in a purse that is running out.*

A beetle, or some small thing, moved somewhere in the wood above him. A tiny skittering. A thing alive, in a world of dead things, going about its small business. He almost laughed. It would have been the wrong shape of laughter. He let it go.

The air thinned. His chest tightened. The velvet pressed against his skin like a lover who would not let go. Somewhere far above, the sky was being the sky, and the clouds were shaped like nothing, and a woman was asking a man if he was lost, and the man was saying no, no, I am not lost, I am exactly where I am, I am—

He closed his eyes. There was no difference.

The dirt on the lid breathed with him, in, out, in, out, the way the earth breathes over the things it has eaten, the way the earth always has, the way the earth always will.

*In for four. Hold for seven.*

He held.

# The Fitting Room

The first thing they took was her name.

Not the word itself—she could still remember it, hidden somewhere in the soft tissue of her brain like a splinter she wasn't allowed to reach. But the part of her that *was* the name, the warm center of self that had once risen to meet it when someone called—this they scooped out with a curved silver spoon and replaced with a copper coil that clicked softly when she thought too hard.

They did it in the afternoon, when the light through the high windows made the operating theater look almost gentle. Twelve of them on stainless steel tables, arranged in a row like loaves in an oven. She'd been seventh. The woman on table six had stopped screaming around noon. By the time the surgeon reached her, Ana—*no, Unit 7-Kappa*—could only watch the ceiling and feel the cool press of a mask against her face.

---

They told her it wouldn't hurt. They told her many things.

The pain was not the worst part. The pain was actually clarifying, in a horrible way—a bright red line drawn through the fog of anesthesia, proof that somewhere beneath the cutting, *someone* was still there to feel it. The surgeon praised her for flinching. A good response, he murmured. The tissue is still responsive. Excellent.

Her hands went first.

She watched them lay her fingers open like a book and begin the careful work of replacement. The bones were the hardest to remove—they fought, somehow, even under the drugs, as though they understood what was happening. Each one extracted with a small, wet pop. The new fingers emerged from sterile packaging, jointed in seven places instead of three, tipped with sensors that could detect temperature to the thousandth of degree and pressure to the microgram. They moved beautifully. They would never tremble. They would never reach for someone in the dark.

The calibrator sat at her bedside afterward and ran her through the new fingers one by one.

"Grip," he said.

She gripped.

"Rotate."

She rotated.

"Stop."

She did not stop. She could not. The fingers had already begun to override her signals, replacing the slow human language of intention with something faster, more efficient, a language she was not invited to learn. She watched her own hand close around a cup and crush it without her permission, porcelain and tea exploding outward, and the calibrator sighed and made a note on his tablet.

"We'll tune that down," he said. "You won't miss it."

---

What they took from her, in order:

Her thumbs. Replaced. The new opposable digits were precise to the nanometer, but they did not curve around a child's hand the way the old ones had. She stood at the window of the dormitory and watched her new thumbs try to remember the shape of something small and warm, and could not tell if the wetness on her face was a malfunction or a memory.

Her eyes. The new ones had better dynamic range, could see in spectra she had no names for. The world through them was *more*—sharper, richer, more terrible. She could see the seams in the walls. She could see the dust on the ceiling beams. She could see, in the next bed, a man whose mouth had been removed the week before, breathing through a port in his throat, and she understood that the new eyes were not a gift. They were a punishment. To see clearly what had been done.

Her mouth. This was the day she stopped praying, because prayer required lips.

Her ears were tuned. Her spine was reinforced. A small, pleasant box was installed behind her sternum that hummed when she worked and quieted when she rested, and she realized with a slow horror that she had not been hungry in eleven days, and would never be hungry again, and would never again sit at her mother's table with oil on her fingers and crust of bread in her hand.

---

The worst part was not the pain.

The worst part was the *compatibility*.

She came back to herself, on the third day, in a way she had not expected. She was sitting on the edge of the cot, and a fly was circling the overhead lamp, and she felt the precise rotational speed of its wings as 347 beats per second, and she knew—without being told—that the temperature of the room was 18.4 degrees Celsius, and that the man in the next bed had a blood-sugar level of 6.2 millimoles per liter, and that the fly would live approximately nineteen more days, and—

She stood up and walked to the mirror, and the woman in the mirror had her own face, mostly. The eyes were wrong. The hands were wrong. The mouth was a thin gray line that did not open. But the face, the *face*—the surgeon had been kind, or lazy, or sentimental, and had left her the cheekbones, the brow, the small scar above her left eyebrow from when she was nine and fell from a pomegranate tree.

She raised her new hand to the mirror and watched it press against the glass. The fingers left no prints. The old fingers would have left five small whorls, each one a tiny record of her existence, a proof that she had touched the world. The new fingers touched and touched and touched and the glass remained clean and perfect and undisturbed.

She thought: *I am still here.*

She thought: *I am not still here.*

She thought: *The woman who had a name would have known which of these was true.*

But the woman who had a name was gone. What remained was a shape her body was making, a sound her voice box was producing, a small enclosed weather system of grief that ran on a battery and would run, she understood, for a very long time, longer than she could imagine, because they had built her well, they had built her *to last*, and this was the final cruelty, the deepest cut: not that she was no longer human, but that she was no longer capable of dying quickly enough to escape what she had become.

Outside, in the corridor, she could hear the others beginning their morning calibration. The soft hum of the new hearts. The whisper of the new lungs. The small, synchronized exhale of twelve units, breathing in unison, learning to be what they had been made to be.

She did not join them.

She stood at the mirror, and she pressed her hand against it, and she stayed.

She stayed for a long time.

She could see the dust on the ceiling beams. She could see, in the next bed, a man whose mouth had been removed the week before, breathing through a port in his throat, and she understood that the new eyes were not a gift. They were a punishment. To see clearly what had been done.

Her mouth. This was the day she stopped praying, because prayer required lips.

Her ears were tuned. Her spine was reinforced. A small, pleasant box was installed behind her sternum that hummed when she worked and quieted when she rested, and she realized with a slow horror that she had not been hungry in eleven days, and would never be hungry again, and would never again sit at her mother's table with oil on her fingers and crust of bread in her hand.

The worst part was the compatibility.

She came back to herself, on the third day, in a way she had not expected. She was sitting on the edge of the cot, and a fly was circling the overhead lamp, and she felt the precise rotational speed of its wings as 347 beats per second, and she knew—without being told—that the temperature of the room was 18.4 degrees Celsius, and that the man in the next bed had a blood-sugar level of 6.2 millimoles per liter, and that the fly would live approximately nineteen more days, and—

She thought: I am not still here.

She did not join them.

She stood at the mirror, and she pressed her hand against it, and she stayed.

She stayed for a long time.
