# The Composition of Silence

Dr. Eleanor Vance had learned to see in negative space.

In her ten years with the Bureau, she had walked into 147 rooms where people had ended other people, and she had developed the unsettling habit of perceiving each one as a tableau vivant—a frozen moment of terrible intention. Her colleagues joked that she was ice, but they didn't understand. The cold wasn't a defense mechanism. It was necessary. You couldn't appreciate the terrible geometry of a thing if you were drowning in it.

It had started with the Hartwell case. A man in a white room, seated at a white table, his blood the only color in the apartment. The arterial spray had fanned across the ceiling in a perfect arc, and Eleanor had stood for eleven minutes before the photographer arrived, unable to speak, because she had never in her life seen such a perfect parabola. The human body, in that final violent moment, had created something mathematically flawless.

She had not slept for three days afterward, not from guilt, but from the fear that she might be sick in some fundamental way.

Now, standing in the doorway of apartment 4B on a Tuesday in October, she felt the familiar tightening in her chest—the one that preceded both dread and the thing she would not name.

The victim was a violinist named Augustus Marsh, sixty-two, found by his neighbor after three days of phone calls left unanswered. The music, the neighbor had said through tears. The music just stopped on Friday.

Eleanor pulled on her gloves and stepped inside.

The light was the first thing. Late afternoon sun through west-facing windows, turned amber by the dust motes that had been left to drift undisturbed for seventy-two hours. It fell in long, honeyed columns that made the apartment look like a Vermeer interior, if Vermeer had ever painted the moment after a man had his throat opened in his sleep. The blood had begun to oxidize, shifting from the bright arterial red of Friday night to the deep burgundy of old wine, and it had spread across the parquet floor in a pattern Eleanor could not immediately parse.

She crouched. The blood was everywhere, but *distributed* everywhere, in a way that suggested not frenzy but intention. It traced the lines between the floorboards, pooling in their grooves like pigment filling channels on a printing block. Augustus Marsh lay in his bed, the wound across his throat so precise it might have been made with a scalpel. A single pillow, untouched. No defensive wounds on the hands. He had not woken.

The killer had not taken anything. The violin still sat in its velvet-lined case in the corner, bow resting inside, rosin untouched. A kitchen table was set for one—dinner half-eaten, a glass of wine, a book turned face-down on a page. The apartment looked like a museum after hours, or a stage struck by the wrong kind of light.

Eleanor moved through the space slowly, and the pattern revealed itself to her in pieces, the way a poem does when you read it twice.

The killer had *arranged* the aftermath. She was certain of it now. The book was open to a specific page—*War and Peace*, the passage about Pierre's captivity and the Platonic Karataev, that meditation on fate and acceptance. The wine glass had been tipped and righted, a single drop running down its stem like a tear. A single white lily, taken from a bouquet by the window, had been laid across the dead man's chest, the way a stone is laid on a grave.

It was a *composition*. A still life of aftermath, built around the body the way an Old Master painter built a Lamentation around a central figure of Christ.

In the corner of the room, near the violin case, the killer had left a single sheet of paper, folded once. Eleanor waited for the evidence team before she unfolded it. She already knew it would contain something—text, an image, a piece of music. The killer would not have been able to resist.

When she finally read it, standing in the hallway while the crime scene techs photographed and measured, she felt the room behind her like a held breath.

It was a haiku.

*Falls the silent string—*
*the bow forgets its purpose;
*what music remains?*

Eleanor stood very still for a long time. Then she folded the paper, slipped it into an evidence bag, and went to make a phone call.

But she carried the image of that room with her through the rest of the week, the way a person carries the melody of a song they cannot stop humming. The lily on the chest. The drop of wine, suspended in its fall. The honeyed light. The book, open to its page.

*Beautiful*, she thought, and then *what is wrong with me*, and then *what is wrong with me that I cannot stop thinking it*.

She dreamed that night of the parabola at Hartwell, and of the lily, and of the silent string. She woke before dawn and went to her office and sat in the dark, and she did not turn on the light for an hour, because she was afraid of what her face might be doing.

Three weeks later, a second violinist was found. A duet this time, the victim holding a bow in his dead hand, the strings of his instrument restrung with what the lab would identify as his own small intestine. A single carnation on the nightstand.

Eleanor stood in that doorway for forty-five minutes.

When she walked out, she told the lead detective: "He's listening to us. He wants us to see him."

What she did not say, what she carried in the silent gallery of her chest: *and he is more talented than I will ever be.*

She began, then, to keep a notebook. Not evidence, not notes. A private record. A catalogue of compositions. She told herself it was for the case. She told herself many things.

The fourth scene was a small church in Vermont. A choir director found at the organ, his hands still on the keys, the choir loft filled with white doves, all of them dead, their necks wrung with the same precision as the throats below. The organ was still playing, one key held down by the weight of a single bird, the same note sustained into the cold morning air.

*Sublime*, Eleanor thought, standing on the threshold, and the word tasted like ash and like honey in equal measure.

She began to understand that the killer was not finished. That the sequence was not yet complete. That somewhere, in a studio or a salon or a concert hall, there was a final room being prepared—the crescendo, the resolution, the key change—and that she, Eleanor, was being invited to attend.

She thought of the haiku. *What music remains.*

She closed the notebook. She did not sleep. In the morning, she would call her supervisor and recommend they accelerate the search, because the pattern suggested the next victim would be a flautist, and the next a cellist, and the next a harpist, and the next a singer, and each room would be more artful than the last, and somewhere in the last room she would find the thing she had been circling for ten years without ever naming.

She did not yet know whether she would arrest the artist or ask to be taught.

In her apartment that night, she played the only recording of Augustus Marsh she could find—a Bach partita, unaccompanied, the Gigue. She listened to the bowing, the lift and fall, the way the bow never quite touched the string, the way the music seemed to fall upward into the air.

When it was over, she sat in the silence that remained, and she let it hold her.

# The Hanging Tree

The cottonwoods stood like black sentinels against the bruise-colored sky, their leaves whispering secrets in a wind that smelled of dust and distant rain. A rope had been thrown over the sturdiest branch that morning, and the noose swayed like a question mark waiting to be answered.

Sheriff Tom Calloway adjusted his hat and looked away from the prisoner. He'd carried out three hangings in his twelve years, and each one had taken a piece of him that never came back. The prisoner—Will Brennan, twenty-six, killer of a storekeeper's wife in Tucumcari—stood on the wagon bed with his hands bound behind him. His boots were new. Someone had given him new boots, and that small kindness troubled the sheriff more than the rest.

A crowd of perhaps forty had gathered. Ranchers in their Sunday worst. Women with dried apricot faces. A boy of about nine who shouldn't have been there but was. The preacher was muttering something Brennan wasn't hearing.

"You got any last words?" the sheriff asked.

Brennan looked up at the rope, then at the sky, then at nothing. "Tell my sister I didn't do it."

Calloway nodded, the way a man nods when he knows the words don't matter anymore. He pulled the black hood down over Brennan's face and stepped back.

"Drive on," he said to the driver.

The horse's hooves clopped once, twice. Then a clatter of hooves on wood and a sharp, percussive sound—not a crack so much as a wet branch snapping underfoot, a sound like a green limb torn from a living tree, intimate and obscene in its finality. A sound that lives in the gut rather than the ears.

The body dropped, swung, and the men who had come to watch let out a collective breath they hadn't known they were holding.

For a long moment, Brennan was still. Then the twitching began.

His fingers curled inward, grasping at the air, at nothing, at the ghost of the pistol he'd fired in the Tucumcari store. His shoulders hitched upward in a shrugging motion, his bound hands jerking at the small of his back as if trying to loosen ropes that were no longer the problem. One polished boot kicked out and then the other, not the wild thrashing of the circus gallows but something smaller, involuntary, the body's last confused attempts to stand on solid ground that wasn't there.

A woman in the front row crossed herself. The preacher began to pray in earnest now, his voice climbing over the creak of the rope. Brennan's head listed to one side, then the other, and his jaw worked beneath the hood as though he were trying to speak. The twitching came in waves, each one weaker than the last, like a wind dying down across an empty plain.

The sheriff watched until it was over. Two minutes. Maybe three. He would never be certain which.

When it was done, he walked to the saloon on the other side of the street and drank until the rope stopped creaking in his memory. It never did, entirely. But the whiskey helped, and the years helped, and the new boots—those damned new boots—somehow helped most of all.

# The Alley Behind Bleecker

The hunger arrived like a second heartbeat.

It pulsed behind Mara's ribs, a hollow, singing thing, and she pressed herself deeper into the alcove behind the dumpster where the brick walls sweated and the only light was a sick sodium-yellow bleeding from a window above. Somewhere, three streets over, a taxi honked. Somewhere farther, a dog barked once and stopped.

The man stumbled into the alley because alleys felt safe to people who only feared other people. He wore a suit jacket, a loosened tie, and the particular brand of exhaustion that came from working too late and drinking not enough water. His keys jingled against his thigh as he walked, the sound small and bright in the wet dark.

Mara watched the vein in his throat. She watched the way his shirt collar moved with each breath. She watched, and she *ached*.

She had fed three nights ago. A woman in a hospital gown who would not be missed. Since then the thirst had built like a fever, drying the back of her tongue, sharpening the world into a single bright needle of want. Every sound came too loud. Every smell came too rich—the soy sauce on his jacket from a hurried dinner, the coffee sour on his breath, the iron-warmth of him, *underneath*, the thick red song of him.

She stepped out.

"Jesus—" He flinched, hand going to his chest, the universal comedy of a frightened man. "You scared me. I didn't see—"

"I'm sorry," she said, and her voice was gentle, and her teeth were already out.

She was on him before he could turn. One hand cupped the back of his head, the other pressed flat against his sternum, pinning him to the cold brick with a strength no woman of her build should have had. He made a small sound—*mmph*—as the air left him, and then she tilted his head, the way you'd tilt a cup, and found the place. The soft triangle where the pulse jumped.

The first puncture was the gentlest. The skin there is so thin it almost welcomes you. A sting, a give, and then the blood rose to meet her like a tide remembering the moon. She sealed her lips over the wound and *drew*, and the world went briefly, beautifully, silent.

He made a sound like a sigh. That was the venom working—the kiss, the older vampires called it, though Mara had never been able to think of it as tender. It was a key turned in a lock. It slid into the wound with the first swallow, a thin hot wire of something that was not quite liquid and not quite air, and it raced through him in the same plumbing the blood was using. She felt him go slack in her arms the way a held bird goes slack—not dead, not gone, just *quieted*, his body suddenly very sure of what was happening and unwilling to fight it.

The second puncture was lower, just above the collarbone, where the vessel ran fat and close. This one hurt him. She felt the flinch ripple through his chest against her palm, a small, distant thing, already belonging to a man who was receding. He tried to speak. She heard the shape of the words, *please* and *why*, but they came out as a long, soft, exhaled vowel.

The hunger unspooled.

It was the only word for it. All the coiled, hissing, clenched thing inside her chest began to loosen, and warmth came pouring into her in slow, thick waves, and with it came *him*—fragments, the way you catch smells from a passing kitchen. Coffee, yes, and the wool of his coat, and beneath that something older, a dog as a child, a father's hand on the back of his neck, a first kiss in a car that smelled like cigarettes, a small and precise fear of heights. These washed through her in a bright cascade and were gone. The blood was a story she would never be able to read in order, and she drank it down like a woman dying of thirst drinks cold water from a cupped hand in a river.

He was trembling. She could feel it through the hand at his sternum—a fine, fast vibration, like a wire struck. His knees were softening. He was a man on the edge of standing up out of a chair, and the chair kept moving. His fingers twitched against the brick. His head grew heavier in her hand, the muscles of his neck forgetting their work.

She eased him down, slowly, so slowly, until he was sitting with his back to the wall and she was kneeling in front of him, and his eyes were open but the man behind them was moving very far away. # The Wounds of Nothing

The first thing Mara feels is wrong.

Not pain—not yet. A displacement. A sense that the air in front of her has *thickened*, the way water thickens when you push your hand into a basin. She stumbles backward, catching herself on a tree, and laughs. The laugh sounds wet and strange in the empty woods.

Then the second thing happens.

Something touches her shoulder. Not a hand—she would know a hand. This is a pressure, an indentation in the meat of her, as though the air itself has grown a thumb and is pressing down, curious, testing the give of her. She slaps at her own shoulder and feels nothing but her palm meeting her shirt.

She runs.

The forest is a cathedral of birch and shadow, and Mara runs through it like a prayer that has forgotten its words. Her boots strike the loam in arrhythmic percussion. Behind her—beside her—*around* her—there is only the absence of sound where sound should be. No crack of branches. No whisper of displaced leaves. Whatever follows her does not belong to the physics of the world she was raised in.

She does not see it. This is the thing that will unmake her.

---

The second wound comes without warning.

Mara feels a line of heat open across her back, as though a single filament of sun has been drawn through her skin. She gasps, arches, and her hand flies to the place. Her fingers come away slick and dark. She stares at them in the green half-light, disbelieving. The blood looks black in shadow.

*Something cut me.*

But there is no blade. There is no claw. There is no mouth. The air where the cut began is empty, and the air where the cut ended is empty, and the wound between is the only proof that anything at all has happened.

She begins to shake. Not from cold.

---

She does not stop running. Stopping has become a word in a language she no longer speaks. Her lungs drag at the air like drowning things. Her calves burn. The birch trunks pass in a pale blur, and she does not know which way is out, only that *out* is a place that must exist, because the alternative is—

The third wound.

This one is in her thigh, deep, a punch of cold that makes her vision strobe white. She falls. The ground meets her with the indifferent hospitality of dirt. She rolls onto her back, breathing through her teeth, and stares up at the canopy where a few pale stars have begun to bruise the sky.

*Look at me,* she thinks. *Whatever you are. Look at me.*

The air does not answer. The air is very good at not answering.

---

Time passes. She does not know how much. She lies in a hollow between roots, her blood seeping into the earth with a sound she can almost hear, and she listens. The forest has grown louder in the way a room grows louder when you know you are not alone in it. Every rustle is a footfall. Every silence is a held breath.

She thinks: *I am being eaten by something I cannot see.*

She thinks: *This is how I will die.*

She thinks: *I don't even know what it looks like. I will never know what it looks like. It will take everything I am and I will not even have the dignity of a face to remember it by.*

A sound reaches her—close, terribly close. Not a growl. Not a hiss. A sound like the inside of a wet mouth. A sound like the word *no* spoken into a pillow.

The fourth wound opens across her ribs. She feels them part, one by one, like a lock being picked. She screams. The scream is hers and she hates it. It is the only thing she can offer in exchange for her own body, and it is not enough, and she knows it is not enough, and the not-enough-ness of it is a horror all its own.

---

She crawls. There is no other word for it. The dignity of running has been taken from her along with the dignity of seeing her killer. She pulls herself through the dirt, leaving a trail behind her like a red ribbon at a terrible festival. Each movement costs her. Each breath costs her. She is being charged for her own life, and the price is not in money but in the slow subtraction of herself.

The fifth wound does not come. The sixth. She waits for them, sobbing, her face pressed into the loam. She waits for the thing she cannot see to finish what it has started. She waits for the wet sound, the displaced air, the clean impossible geometry of being opened by nothing.

The forest breathes. The stars drift. Somewhere, an owl calls out a question that no one will answer.

Mara lies in the hollow of the roots, bleeding, and realizes with a clarity that tastes like iron that she has been granted a reprieve and does not know why. The thing has chosen to stop. The thing has looked at her—*felt* at her?—and decided she is not yet finished.

She closes her eyes. The darkness behind her lids is no different from the darkness in the air.

She waits.

The thing, unseen, waits too.

# The Choosing

The courtyard smelled of rain and iron. Mara stood in the center of the flagstones, her hands bound in front of her, and tried to remember how to breathe.

Before her stood three posts. Before the posts stood three of her friends.

Elena, who had taught her to read when she was seven, who still tucked a sprig of dried lavender into her braid each morning out of habit. She had not stopped doing this even now. Even with the rope around her neck. The little purple stem trembled against her collarbone.

Davit, who had carried her half a mile through the flood when the river took the village, who had argued with her about poetry and lost gracefully and cooked for her when she could not rise from bed. He was weeping openly. He did not try to hide it. He had never tried to hide anything in his life.

Saren, who had betrayed her. Who had told the soldiers where to find the resistance. Who had looked her in the eye two nights ago and said *I am sorry, Mara, I am so sorry, they have my sister, they have my little sister* and had meant it, had meant every wretched word of it.

The Commandant's voice came again, flat and unhurried, as though he were ordering wine. "One. You may select one. The other two will hang at dawn. Choose, and the chosen one walks free. Refuse, and all three swing before the sun is up. You have until that bell finishes ringing."

The bell had begun. Each slow toll was a small eternity.

Mara's mind moved in the way minds move when they cannot bear what is in front of them — sideways, into small irrelevant things. *I am standing on the third flagstone from the well. Elena's hem is fraying at the left side. Davit's left shoe is untied. Saren's wrists are bleeding where the rope is too tight.* These were the thoughts of a woman who had been split into a thousand pieces and was trying, with whatever scrap of herself still held together, to find the seam that would let her reassemble.

*You cannot do this. You cannot do this. You cannot do this.*

But the bell kept tolling.

She looked at Elena. *If I save her, she will spend the rest of her life wondering why. She will not sleep. She will not eat. She will stand in doorways and look at her hands and think — I lived because my friend killed two people in front of me.* And worse: *I will be the one who did it to her.*

She looked at Davit. *If I save him, he will understand. He has always understood. He is the one who would forgive me. He is the one who would come to me afterward and put his hand on my shoulder and say nothing, because he knows there is nothing to say.* And that was worse. Because she knew he would do that. And that knowledge made the choice heavier, not lighter.

She looked at Saren. *If I save her, I am rewarding betrayal. I am saying that what she did was worth forgiving because she asked prettily enough. I am saying that a child's life weighs more than the friends she sold to save it. I am saying that love is an excuse, and it is not, and it is.* And worse: *I will spend every day of the rest of my life asking her — did I do right? And she will have to answer me. And I will have to live with the answer.*

The bell was on its seventh toll. The eighth. The ninth.

"Choose," said the Commandant, as if reminding her to pass the salt.

Mara opened her mouth. No sound came. She closed it. She tried again. She could feel her own pulse in her throat, enormous, absurd, as though her heart were trying to climb out of her body and run.

"Elena," she said, and the word came out as a sound she had never made before, the sound of a woman tearing a piece out of herself and handing it away.

The bell finished.

---

She did not watch. She had said she would not, and she kept the promise to herself, which was the only promise left to her. But she heard. She heard the singing — the hymn, the one they sang at the river, the one Davit's mother used to hum when she was hanging the washing. They sang it together, the three of them, in ragged unison, and the sound of it was the most terrible and the most beautiful thing she had ever heard, and she thought *I will hear this until I die, and after I die, and after the world is ash.*

She heard the creak of the platform tilting. She heard the small, soft sounds that bodies make when they have only just stopped being alive — not the ones from the songs, not the great dramatic ones, but the smaller ones, the click of a heel against wood, the exhale that no one answers.

Then silence. Then the sound of her own breathing, which was now the loneliest sound in the world.

Elena stood beside her in the grey morning. Elena's hand found hers. Elena's hand was shaking so badly that Mara could not feel her own fingers inside it.

Neither of them spoke. There was nothing in any language that any human being had ever spoken that was large enough for this.

Elena would, in time, walk away. She would go south. She would live, for sixty more years, and she would never again tuck lavender into her braid. She would smell it, once, on a hillside in late summer, and she would fall to her knees in the grass, and a stranger would find her there and not know what to do. That is how it would end for Elena. It would never end for Elena.

Mara would live too. That was the worst of it. She would live, and she would wake each morning, and she would have to be a person, and the person she would have to be was a woman who had done this. She would carry it the way a stone is carried in the chest — not heavy in the way of grief, which can be set down, but heavy in the way of a thing that has become the body itself. The choosing would not be a memory. It would be her skeleton. It would be the bones of her face, the bones of her hands, the architecture of every breath she took for the rest of her life.

She had been asked to choose between her friends.

She had not understood, until the bell finished ringing, that there had been no choice at all — only four ways to be destroyed.

The tier itself groaned as inmates rushed its length in a desperate charge, the steel railings flexing under the weight of human mass. There was only *us* and *them* now, and *them* was anyone in a uniform.

A guard in the riot control unit appeared at the far end of the corridor, gas mask pulled down, shotgun raised. He fired one canister into the crowd, and the advancing mass parted around it like water around a stone. The CS gas bloomed, white and acrid, but these were men who had learned to fight through worse. Eyes streaming, some of them didn't even blink. The ones who did simply blinked faster, and kept coming.

The PA system crackled to life, then died, then crackled again—administrators somewhere in the secure wing trying to restore order to a building that had forgotten what order meant. In a corner of the dayroom, two inmates fought each other—not guards, but each other. Old debts being settled in the only currency the prison ever truly accepted. Blood on the concrete, blood on their hands, blood on the gray uniforms that were no longer gray. The sound of it was the same sound it had always been in places like this: meat and bone, the wet percussion of human violence, as old as the stones of the walls that contained them.

Above it all, the lights kept flashing. Red, red, red. The heartbeat of a facility in cardiac arrest.

# The Marriott, Room 412

The TV was tuned to some home renovation show. A woman in a hard hat was explaining backsplash options to a man who looked like he regretted every decision that led him to this moment.

Daria sat cross-legged on one of the double beds, a disassembled Glock 19 spread across the white comforter like surgical instruments. She was working a nylon brush through the barrel with the focused calm of someone cleaning a pipe.

Marco was at the small table by the window, a mug of black coffee steaming beside him. He was reassembling a suppressed Beretta, fingers moving with the absent ease of a man who'd done this ten thousand times. Outside, the city went about its evening.

"You know what I love?" Daria said, not looking up. "Lodging. It's elegant. No mess, no fuss."

Marco snorted. "Of course you do. You've got a soft spot for the old ways."

"There's a reason they're old." She set down the brush and reached for the cleaning patches. "One phone call, one location, one bullet, and by the time anyone finds them they're cold. The paperwork, the surveillance, the *thinking*—all gone. I like that. There's a tidiness to it."

"Sticks. Yeah." He thumbed the slide back on the Beretta, checked the resistance, nodded to himself. "Me, I'm more of a long-distance guy. Optics, windage, a half-mile of empty air between me and them. By the time they hear the report, they're already part of the soil report."

"Distant."

"Professional," he corrected. He picked up his coffee, blew across the top. "And you get to see the scenery. Last one I took was in Montenegro. I was set up in this shepherd's hut, and the sun was coming up over the bay, and—"

"Are you seriously telling me about the *view*?"

"I take pride in my work, Daria. The placement matters, the preparation matters, the *aesthetic* matters. Why do you think I only use suppressed .22s? The report should be a whisper. A confession."

She rolled her eyes, slotting the slide back onto her Glock's frame. "You romanticize everything."

"And you don't?"

She considered. "Sometimes the car bomb has a certain poetry. The temperature of the ignition. The way the windows blow out in a perfect star pattern. There's a small satisfaction in that." She clicked the magazine home, set the weapon on the nightstand. "But mostly I just like that it's done before they know it started. They had a whole day ahead of them—coffee, emails, a meeting at three—and now they don't."

Marco was quiet for a moment, sipping his coffee. On the TV, the couple was arguing about whether to demo a wall.

"It's a job," he said finally. "That's the thing people don't get. You make it into this big, dramatic thing, but it's a job. Some guy installs HVAC. You and I handle contracts. You clock in, you do the work, you clock out."

"Don't say *clock in* like that. It makes it sound like we're at a factory."

"You know what I mean." He wiped a smudge off the Beretta's suppressor with the corner of the bedspread. "The man who hired us has a problem. We solve the problem. Everyone goes home. Clean."

"Until next time," Daria said.

"Until next time."

The home renovation couple had agreed on subway tile. Marco turned back to his coffee. Outside, a siren wailed somewhere far away, and then didn't.

The wood crackles first—a hungry, spitting sound, like a thousand whispering voices. Sparks spiral upward into a sky that offers no witness. The heat arrives in waves, pressing against exposed skin before the flames even reach their mark, a warning the body understands before the mind does.

Then comes the smoke. It doesn't rise cleanly. It coils, thick and black, tasting of pitch and char and something older. It fills the lungs with a weight that is not quite pain but the promise of it. The eyes stream. The world becomes a smear of orange glow and dark, wavering shapes—the crowd, the priest, the sky—shadows at the edges of a closing circle.

The first scream is not the loudest. It is the first one that breaks through shock, sharp and animal, the sound of a person meeting the unbearable and refusing to accept it. The body thrashes. The ropes hold. Smoke pours from the pyre in dark, oily columns, and the screams continue, ragged now, each one a little shorter, a little higher, a little more thin.

The heat by then is no longer heat but pressure—a weight of air that pushes in from every side, drying the throat, cracking the lips, turning breath itself into a small burning. The figures in the crowd grow distant, their murmuring fading beneath the roar. The flames are louder than the voices now, louder than the screaming, though the screaming goes on—quieter, wetter, a sound less of voice than of will refusing to stop.

Then, eventually, a final sound. Not a scream anymore. A sigh. The body, which had been a person, sags against the stake. The smoke keeps rising. The crowd begins to disperse, pulling cloaks tighter, walking home through the dark.

# The Carrion Hymn

The moon hung swollen and green over the moor, a bloated thing that seemed to watch with something like hunger. Across the black expanse of heather and frost-brittled bone-orchards, hundreds of holes gaped in the earth—fresh-dug graves, their contents unearthed and laid out in concentric rings around a shallow basin of obsidian. The dead of three villages lay there in their rows, each one wrapped in burial linen gone the color of weak tea, each one already beginning to bloat beneath the shroud.

Veyla knelt at the basin's edge.

She was thin as a penance. Her face was a skull wearing skin, hollows beneath her cheekbones deep enough to hide a finger, and her eyes—her eyes were the worst part, for they had no whites anymore, only a sclera of black and irises the pale violet of a bruise. Her lips moved constantly, even in silence, as if chewing on words too bitter to swallow. Her hands, long-fingered and ink-stained to the second knuckle, hovered above the dark water that filled the basin. The water was not water. It was thick, and it moved of its own accord, and it smelled of pennies and turned earth and the sweet rot of a mouth that had stopped being a mouth.

*Come up,* she thought. *Come up, come up, my darlings, my sweet children of the worm.*

The first to move was a child.

She could not have been more than seven when they put her in the ground. Her name had been Aelis, though Veyla did not know this, and did not care to. The linen over her belly rose once, twice, like the chest of something dreaming, and then a hand—small, blue-nailed, the skin of it going to a kind of gray parchment where it had not yet burst—broke through the cloth and reached for the sky. The fingers curled and uncurled, curled and uncurled, like the legs of a beetle on its back.

Veyla smiled, and the smile was the saddest thing in the world.

"That's it, little one. Wake up. Wake up for Mother."

The wrongness began in the bones. Veyla felt it like a hook in her own spine, a wrongness that was not pain but the *memory* of pain, the shape of pain turned inside out. The dead did not want to rise. There was a forgetting in the grave, a blessed dark where nothing wanted anything, and to drag a thing back from that was to drag it back from *itself*. She had done it a thousand times, and it was never easy, and it was never kind, and the smallness of the child in the shroud made no difference, for Veyla's heart had been taken out of her long ago and replaced with something that beat and pumped but did not love.

The child's eyes opened.

They were not the eyes of a child. They were not the eyes of anything that had ever been alive. The pupils had gone a milky amber, and they glowed faintly from within, like lanterns buried in snow. The mouth fell open and from it came a sound—not a cry, not a word, but a kind of wet clicking, the sound of a throat trying to remember how speech was shaped. The body sat up in stages, like a puppet hauled upright on broken strings. Stiff. Wrong. The joints moved in directions that joints should not move.

And then came the second, and the third, and the twentieth, and the hundredth, and the moor was filled with the sound of a thousand people learning to breathe again, and none of them breathed, and none of them needed to, and the noise they made was worse than screaming because it sounded like a lullaby played on a broken music box.

# The Last Course

The candle between us catches a draft and leans, throwing new shadows across his face. He doesn't notice. He's telling me about his daughter's piano recital, waving his fork for emphasis, and I nod in the right places while watching his throat.

I chose the vintage carefully. It's the kind of detail a person like him would appreciate—ironic, really, given the circumstances. He praised the bouquet when he first sat down. *A man who knows his tannins*, he said, and I thought: yes, I do. I know exactly what's in it.

I watch him take another bite of the rack of lamb, and I calculate. Five minutes since the second glass. The first symptoms are usually subtle—a warmth in the chest, perhaps, the kind one might attribute to good wine and the company of an old friend.

He sets down his fork and laughs at something I've said, something I can't even remember because I have not been listening to my own words. I have been listening to his breathing. There—faster now. A slight hitch at the top of each inhale. I press my napkin to my lips so he cannot see my mouth working around a smile I cannot control.

"More wine?" I ask, and he declines, and this is the part where a less experienced person might panic. But I have accounted for two glasses. Three would have been careless. The dose is precise, and precision is what separates an artist from a butcher.

"You look a little flushed," I offer, leaning forward with the concern I have practiced for weeks. "The room is warm, isn't it?"

He agrees, loosening his collar. His fingers are trembling slightly, and he notices this too, because he laughs again and says something about the wine being stronger than it seemed. He does not yet understand. That will come in a moment, when the heat in his chest becomes a pressure, and the pressure becomes something he cannot name.

I take a slow sip from my own glass, the untainted one I poured when his back was turned. I make a point of commenting on the main course, on the chef's use of rosemary, on anything at all, because silence now would unnerve even a man not feeling the first dark fingers of what I have put inside him.

"I think perhaps—" he begins, and then pauses. His hand goes to his sternum. An absent gesture, the way one might brush away a fly. But there is no fly.

"Digestion," I supply helpfully. "Lamb can be heavy."

He nods slowly. The sweat has begun at his temples, beading along the hairline, and his pupils have widened to swallow the candlelight. I watch this and I feel, I confess, what I have come to recognize as my own particular affliction—not guilt, not pleasure, but a kind of terrible focus. The way a surgeon must feel at the first incision. The way an architect feels when the first stone is laid and the building has begun, and there is nothing left to do but let gravity and time do their work.

"You seem tired," I say softly, and I reach across the white linen to place my hand over his. The skin under my palm is damp, fevered. He looks at our hands together and does not pull away. This is the last kindness I will ever show him, and I make myself feel it fully—the weight of his fingers, the faint pulse beneath them, the warmth that will not be warmth much longer.

"The lamb," he murmurs. "It didn't sit right, I think."

He will not finish his sentence. Not because he cannot, but because what is happening to him has begun to outpace language, to outpace everything. His breathing is shallower now. The flush has spread down his throat, and he is gripping the edge of the table the way a man grips a railing on a tilting ship.

I do not call for help. Not yet. There is a rhythm to these things, and I have learned to honor it.

Outside, through the tall window behind him, the city lights glitter in their thousands, and each one is a life going on without witness, and each one is unremarkable, and I wonder, watching the last of the light leave his eyes in its slow procession, whether any of them know what it is to be the only other person in a room and the only one who understands what is happening.

He tries to speak. I lean close, as a friend would, as a concerned companion, and I hold his gaze until the moment comes when there is no one left behind it to look back at me.

Only then do I pour myself the last of the wine and raise it to my lips.

Only then do I begin, very quietly, to weep.

# The Reckoning

The morning sun rose crimson over the Crimson Harlot, but no man aboard found beauty in it. The crew had been summoned to the main deck, and now they stood in a grim semicircle, their eyes fixed on a single figure bound at the wrists.

Jonas Ketch, boatswain of the Harlot, knelt on the salt-crusted planks. His lip was split. His eyes were wild. He had been caught trying to release the bilge-caged powder barrels belowdecks—had been caught whispering to three others about opening the captain's cabin by nightfall and taking the helm.

Captain Thaddeus Vex stood before him, thumbs hooked in his belt, a man carved from leather and old grievance. He did not shout. He had not shouted once in twenty years of piracy, and that was what frightened the men far more than any roar.

"Ketch," he said, quiet as a tide turning. "You know what we do with rats."

"It weren't—I never—" Ketch's words tumbled over themselves. His voice cracked on the second syllable. "Cap'n, I was drunk. I was mad. I'd never have—"

"You were sober when you loaded the pistols." Vex gestured to a small chest, recently broken open. "You were sober when you drew the map of my cabin door. You were sober, Jonas, when you asked Berrick how many grains of powder would blow a man's skull clean off."

Ketch began to weep. Not prettily. The kind of weeping that makes a man look younger and smaller and more pathetic than he has any right to be.

"Get him up."

Two of the crew—men who had been his conspirators the night before, who had given him up at the first whiff of the cat—hauled Ketch to his feet. His knees were gray and trembling. He looked at the horizon, at the open water, and understood.

The sharks had been following the Harlot for three days. Every sailor knew the signs: the dark fins cutting slow arcs in the vessel's wake, the great shadows drifting beneath the hull like submerged sails. The cook had stopped gutting fish over the side, because the frenzy that followed made the men sick to their stomachs.

The plank was a length of pine, perhaps fourteen feet long, lashed at its inner end to the rail and jutted out over the gunwale, pointing at nothing but a long, slow fall into the green-and-black water. A man could see the shadows from up there. A man could see the way they turned, almost lazily, as if they had all the time in the world.

They had all the time in the world. He did not.

Ketch was led to the plank. At its base, he stopped, and his body became a thing made entirely of refusal. He planted his bare feet and pulled backward with everything he had, and the two men holding him had to lean into the rope. The sound he made was not a word. It was the sound a man makes when he has run out of words and is left only with the animal knowledge of what waits below.

"Cap'n—" This was all he had. "Cap'n, please—"

Vex watched him. There was no pleasure in the captain's face. There was not even anger, not anymore. There was only the long, cold arithmetic of a ship that could not afford a second mutiny.

"Walk," said Vex.

Ketch took a step. The plank dipped. Below, a shadow turned.

He took another step. He was crying so hard that the tears and the spray became one thing on his face. He could see them now, more clearly than he had ever wanted to see anything—three, four, five dark crescents circling in the indigo. One broke the surface, briefly, and the glimpse of its underbelly, that milk-white crescent, was the worst thing he had ever seen.

He tried to turn. He could not. There was no turning back from a plank, and that was the point of a plank.

He made a sound—half prayer, half howl—and the sound carried out over the water, and out over the water something answered. Not a sound, exactly. A presence. A great slow mass, rising.

"Please—" he whispered. "Please, God, please—"

Vex looked at him. Then, with one small gesture, he nodded to the men behind Ketch.

They stepped forward.

Ketch's bare feet left the pine. For a single, stretched moment he was in the air, his arms pinwheeling, his face turned up to a sky that did not care. Then the water took him.

The splash was smaller than a man would have thought.

For a moment, nothing. He came up thrashing, screaming, his bound hands flailing at the surface. The shadows were still distant. A man, he thought wildly. A man can swim. A man can— 

The first shape came from beneath him. He felt it before he saw it—the immense, smooth rush of something impossibly large moving under his legs, lifting him bodily, then rolling. The scream that left him then was not a word in any language. It was a sound the sea itself might have made, if the sea could speak.

The water turned. Not all at once. In patches. In blooms. A cloud the color of a darkening sky, spreading outward from where he had been.

Ketch screamed again, and the scream was shorter. And shorter still. His hand broke the surface once—open, reaching, the fingers spread wide as if he were trying to grasp the empty air. The fingers curled. The hand sank.

Below, the water moved with terrible, unhurried purpose. Something pale rolled at the surface—a fragment, briefly, before it was pulled under again. A ragged shape, not recognizable as anything that had ever been a man. Then that, too, was gone.

The great shadow rose once, very slowly, just beneath the hull of the Harlot. A single black eye, ancient and depthless, regarded the ship. Then it sank, and the water closed over it like a shutting eye, and the sea was smooth again.

No one on the deck spoke. The only sound was the slap of water against the hull and, distantly, the cry of a gull that knew nothing and cared about nothing.

Captain Vex drew a long breath. He looked at the men. Some of them were pale. Some of them were dry-eyed and hard. He could use the hard ones. The pale ones he would watch.

"That's done," he said quietly. "Back to stations."

The crew dispersed. The plank was drawn back aboard. A board boy was sent below to scrub it, and by sunset the wood was pale and clean again, and the ship moved on through waters that, for once, were empty of fins.

But for a long while after, the men did not fish over the side. And when they walked the deck at night, they did not look down.

He planted his bare feet and pulled backward with everything he had, and the two men holding him had to lean into the rope. The sound he made was not a word. It was the sound a man makes when he has run out of words and is left only with the animal knowledge of what waits below.

"Cap'n—" This was all he had. "Cap'n, please—"

Vex watched him. There was no pleasure in the captain's face. There was not even anger, not anymore. There was only the long, cold arithmetic of a ship that could not afford a second mutiny.

"Walk," said Vex.

Ketch took a step. The plank dipped. Below, a shadow turned.

He took another step. He was crying so hard that the tears and the spray became one thing on his face. He could see them now, more clearly than he had ever wanted to see anything—three, four, five dark crescents circling in the indigo. One broke the surface, briefly, and the glimpse of its underbelly, that milk-white crescent, was the worst thing he had ever seen.

He tried to turn. He could not. There was no turning back from a plank, and that was the point of a plank.

He made a sound—half prayer, half howl—and the sound carried out over the water, and out over the water something answered. Not a sound, exactly. A presence. A great slow mass, rising.

"Please—" he whispered. "Please, God, please—"

Vex looked at him. Then, with one small gesture, he nodded to the men behind Ketch.

They stepped forward.

Ketch's bare feet left the pine. For a single, stretched moment he was in the air, his arms pinwheeling, his face turned up to a sky that did not care. Then the water took him.

The splash was smaller than a man would have thought.

For a moment, nothing. He came up thrashing, screaming, his bound hands flailing at the surface. The shadows were still distant. A man, he thought wildly. A man can swim. A man can—

The first shape came from beneath him. He felt it before he saw it—the immense, smooth rush of something impossibly large moving under his legs, lifting him bodily, then rolling. The scream that left him then was not a word in any language. It was a sound the sea itself might have made, if the sea could speak.

The water turned. Not all at once. In patches. In blooms. A cloud the color of a darkening sky, spreading outward from where he had been.

Ketch screamed again, and the scream was shorter. And shorter still. His hand broke the surface once—open, reaching, the fingers spread wide as if he were trying to grasp the empty air. The fingers curled. The hand sank.

The great shadow rose once, very slowly, just beneath the hull of the Harlot. A single black eye, ancient and depthless, regarded the ship. Then it sank, and the water closed over it like a shutting eye, and the sea was smooth again.

# The Rattle of the Empty House

---

The first night, the faucet dripped in triplets.

Eleanor had installed new washers in both bathrooms just last Tuesday. She knew this because she'd stood in the hardware aisle at Lowe's for forty minutes, reading the back of blister packs while her phone buzzed with calls she couldn't bring herself to answer. New washers. Brand new. The dripping, then, was not a washer.

It was a pattern.

*Tap. Tap-tap.*

She lay in bed and stared at the ceiling, which she'd also just painted. *Benjamin Moore Decorator's White, eggshell finish.* She remembered because she'd watched the paint dry, the way it had slowly gone from wet gray to a brilliant, sterile white. Three coats. The ceiling was fresh, sealed, finished, and above her it began, very faintly, to *breathe*.

She did not turn on the light. She did not move. She lay very still, the way prey lies still, and pretended to sleep until her bones ached with the pretense.

In the morning, the faucet was dry.

---

The second night, she found a single muddy shoeprint on the kitchen tile.

Her kitchen was spotless. She cleaned it the way other people prayed — daily, ritualistically, with a kind of desperate gratitude. There was no mud in the house. There was no mud in her life. She lived alone. She owned no shoes that could make such a print. The tread was a herringbone pattern she didn't recognize, the size of a man's foot, and the mud was black and smelled, when she crouched down and pressed her nose near it, of river silt and something sweeter underneath. Something coppery. Something she refused to name.

She cleaned it. She cleaned it with bleach, then with vinegar, then with her bare hands, scrubbing until her knuckles split and bled. She did not stop. The shoeprint came back. It came back every morning, always in a different place — once by the refrigerator, once at the foot of the stairs, once directly in front of the bathroom mirror, where she stood and looked down at it and saw, just for a moment, the reflection of someone standing behind her.

She did not turn around.

She was not ready to turn around.

---

On the fifth night, he started to speak.

It began as a sound she thought was the house settling — the old sighing that houses do, the wooden bones of them shifting in the dark. But the houses she had known in her life had not had voices. This one did. The voice was low, and patient, and it spoke in the third person, the way people speak about the dead.

*"Eleanor is afraid."*

She sat up in bed. The bedroom was dark. The windows were dark. The hallway beyond the bedroom door was dark, and from that dark came the words, drifting toward her like smoke.

*"Eleanor did a bad thing."*

She had a gun in the nightstand. She had owned it for eleven years, ever since the night she had driven into the culvert off Miller's Road and walked back to a house that no longer held a body. She had never once fired it. She had never once needed to. Until now, the gun had been a kind of talisman — a thing that existed to be *not used*, the way a fence exists to be *not jumped*.

Her hand moved toward the drawer. The voice, in the hallway, waited.

*"Eleanor took a man from the world."*

Her hand stopped.

*"Eleanor is going to give him back."*

---

By the second week, she had stopped sleeping.

This was a choice. She had calculated it the way you might calculate the dosage of a dangerous medicine: not enough, and the sickness wins; too much, and you kill the patient. Three hours. Four, at most. Any more than that, and the *dreams* started — and the dreams were worse than the waking, because in the dreams she was not alone.

In the dreams, she was back in the culvert. In the dreams, his face was the color of the moon and his eyes were open and they *knew her*. In the dreams, he reached up from the muck at the bottom of the ditch and touched her wrist with fingers that were cold and very, very patient.

In the waking, she heard him in the walls. In the waking, she found things she had hidden years ago: a button from his coat, a receipt for a tank of gas, a Polaroid she had burned and buried and now found, somehow, slipped between the pages of a cookbook she hadn't opened in a decade. The Polaroid was always curling at the edges. The Polaroid was always *smiling*.

She stopped cooking. She stopped eating. She drank black coffee and watched the sun come up, and when the sun came up, the house was quiet, and she was almost a person.

Almost.

---

The third week, she saw him in the mirror.

She was brushing her teeth. The bathroom was bright. The bulbs were daylight-spectrum, five thousand Kelvin, the kind of light that flattens a face into a mask. She was brushing her teeth with great, deliberate strokes, watching herself the way you watch a stranger through a window.

The man in the mirror behind her was *not* a stranger.

He was standing in the bathtub. He was wearing the clothes he had been wearing when she had — he was wet. He was dripping. He was smiling the way the Polaroid was smiling, the way a thing smiles when it has all the time in the world and nothing left to lose.

She did not scream. She had not screamed in eleven years. Screaming, she had decided, was a luxury reserved for people who had not yet done what she had done. She set down the toothbrush. She turned off the tap. She turned, very slowly, on the damp tile.

The bathtub was empty.

She looked back at the mirror. He was closer. He was right behind her. She could smell him — river silt, copper, and underneath it, something green and sweet, the smell of waterlogged earth. She could feel his breath on the back of her neck, cold, the breath of something that did not need to breathe.

*"Eleanor."*

This time, he said her name in *first* person. He said it the way he had said it the night she — the way he had said it *once*, in life, in the moment before —

She ran.

---

She ran to the kitchen and she called 911 and she said, *"There is a man in my house."*

The dispatcher was calm. The dispatcher asked if the man was armed. The dispatcher asked if the man had hurt her. The dispatcher asked for her address, and Eleanor gave it, and the dispatcher said officers were on the way, and Eleanor said, *"Hurry. Hurry. He was in the bathtub. He's in the house. He has been in the house for —"*

She stopped.

*"Ma'am? Are you still there?"*

She looked down at the kitchen counter. There, in the weak dawn light, was a small mound of river mud, and in the mud, as if a child had pressed it there with a careless thumb, was a single perfect print.

A *handprint*.

Small. A child's hand. The fingers splayed.

There was no child.

There had *never* been a child.

The dispatcher was saying something. Eleanor was not hearing her. Eleanor was looking at the handprint, and the handprint was moving, and the handprint was *crawling* across the counter, leaving a thin glistening trail, and at the end of the hand, where the wrist would have been, there was only more mud, more dark, and from the dark came the voice, very close now, very gentle, the way you speak to a frightened animal.

*"Eleanor. I'm not in the house."*

A long pause. The handprint reached the edge of the counter. It paused there, as if considering the drop.

*"I've been inside you the whole time."*

---

The police found her at dawn.

She was on the kitchen floor, in the position of a woman who had been praying, except that her hands were not clasped. Her hands were at her throat. Her face was the color of the moon. Her eyes were open. Her eyes *knew them*.

There was no sign of a struggle. There was no sign of another person. There was only Eleanor, on the floor of a house that smelled faintly of river silt and something sweeter underneath, something the paramedics would not be able to name, and a handprint in the mud on the counter, and another on the wall, and another on the ceiling above where she lay, and all of them, every single one, were *crawling* slowly inward, toward the place where her body had finally, after eleven years, gone still.

The officers did not stay long.

None of them could explain why. None of them would ever be able to. They simply looked at Eleanor's face, and at the handprints, and at the way the dawn light was falling through the kitchen window, and they *left*.

Later, in the report, they would write that the scene had been *unsettling*. Later, in their dreams, they would smell river silt and copper and something green and sweet. Later, they would wake at three in the morning, and they would lie very still, and they would listen, with terrible attention, for the sound of something *breathing* in the walls of their own houses.

The house stood empty after that.

It stands empty still.

And if you drive by, late at night, on the road that used to be Miller's Road, you will see, in the upstairs window, a light that should not be there. You will see, for just a moment, the silhouette of a woman, standing very still, her hands at her throat, her face turned toward the dark.

You will see her mouth move.

You will not hear what she is saying.

But if you are quiet, and if you listen, and if you *lean in close enough* —

You will hear him answer.

---

*"Eleanor."*

The rain hadn't started yet, but I could smell it in the air—that particular mix of wet concrete and forgotten things the city exhales when it's about to drown itself. I lit a cigarette I didn't want and looked down at what's left of Arthur Wexley.

Poor bastard.

He was spread out on his office floor like a question nobody wanted to answer, his blood already blackening into the weave of the carpet. The red had gone that awful rust color, the way a sunset goes when the city chews it up and spits it out somewhere over the river. Somebody had taken to him with enthusiasm—the kind of enthusiasm that says *personal*—and what remained was less a man than a geography. A topography of damage, the kind the urban planners could study if they wanted to understand what the underside of a city really looks like.

I crouched down. The knees of my trousers darkened against whatever it was I was kneeling in, and I made a mental note not to bother with the cleaners this month.

Wexley's eyes were still open, staring at the ceiling like he was waiting for an answer from the fluorescent lights. The ones above him were flickering—one of those dying bulbs that buzz and stutter, throwing shadows in all the wrong places, the way a neighborhood does when it's three weeks past payday and the landlord has stopped pretending to fix the elevator. The light made his face look like something dredged from a storm drain after the third flood of the season. Something the water had worked on for a while. Something the city had almost finished digesting.

The wound in his chest was a kind of mouth, working its silent testimony into the carpet fibers. A door that only opened one way now. I'd seen my share of doors like that. Everybody in this line of work has. You learn to read them the way a sailor reads weather.

His suit was good. Not great, but good—the kind of mid-tier confidence a man wears when he's risen just high enough to be visible and not high enough to be safe. I straightened up and looked out the window. Down on the street, a neon sign for a diner was shorting out, its pink light bleeding and rebleeding across the wet asphalt, flickering like a pulse nobody was monitoring. A cab slid past through a puddle. Somewhere a dog was barking at something that wasn't there.

Wexley had been trying to tell someone something. That's always how it goes. Everybody in this town is trying to tell someone something, and most of them die with the words still trapped behind their teeth, fermenting. The city collects these little unfinished sentences the way it collects everything else—garbage, ambition, bodies, dreams. Piles them up in some forgotten lot where the streetlights don't reach and lets the rats sort it out.

I took a drag of the cigarette and let the smoke out slow, watching it curl toward the ceiling and get eaten by the fluorescent hum.

*Alright, Artie*, I thought. *You're a long way from finished telling me. You just don't know it yet.*

Somewhere down the block, a garbage truck groaned into gear, and the rain finally started—soft at first, then harder, the way this city always does things. Like it has something to prove.

I flicked ash onto the floor. I was already late, and the dead don't care about being polite.

Nobody in this town does.

# The Eleventh Hour

The scent wall hit her first—pine resin, ozone, and something metallic that Vela couldn't name but had learned to dread. The artificial forest stretched for fifty kilometers in every direction, its trees a patchwork of real specimens and printed facsimiles, all maintained by a climate system that hummed beneath the soil like a sleeping god.

Vela pressed her back against a holographic outcropping that shimmered with convincing moss. Her breath came in shallow draws. The tracker embedded beneath her left scapula pulsed a faint, accusatory blue—she could feel it warming against her muscle, the way a tooth aches before the rain.

Eleven hours she'd been running. Eleven hours since the gates had opened and seventy-three runners had scattered like startled quail into the Preserves.

Now there were forty-one.

She checked the map. Her wrist display flickered—good signal here, a quirk of the valley's topology that she'd been exploiting all day. The safe zone contracted another three kilometers in forty minutes. There was a river crossing she could make, a thermal vent where the scanners went blind for precisely ninety seconds, a hollow beneath a fallen synthetic oak where she'd cached water six hours ago and prayed no one else had found it.

She began to move.

---

The hunter, whose public name was Cassian Vex but whose private name no longer mattered to anyone, had not moved in four hours.

He sat in a blind he'd constructed from thermal-reactive mesh, fifty meters up in a real white pine—the system allowed authentic trees in pockets, a concession to "wilderness authenticity" that the Syndicate's psychologists had recommended. The blind was invisible to standard scans, dampened to body temperature, and so still that two chickadees had landed on its edge and begun a territorial argument directly above his head.

Vex did not watch the ground. Ground-work was for amateurs, for the chasers who relied on noise and tracker signatures. Vex watched the patterns.

He had a console on his knee displaying every runner's projected vector, updated in real-time from the fleet of drones that made the Preserve less a forest than a living diorama. Each runner appeared as a small amber light, drifting through the green topology of the map like a school of phosphorescent fish.

He watched Vela's light. He had been watching Vela's light for three hours.

She was, he had to admit, exceptional. She had refused the northern meadow—too exposed. She had avoided the river—too predictable. She had used the thermal vents twice, which only one runner in a hundred remembered to exploit, and she had done so without hesitation, as if she had studied the topography in advance.

*Competitors,* he thought, without rancor. *Or perhaps a veteran.*

There was no telling. The Syndicate was creative with its sourcing. Last season, the runners had included a former Minister of Atmospheric Affairs, three convicted dissidents, and, memorably, a child of one of the Showcase families who had been "volunteered" after a televised scandal. The public loved the storylines. Betting markets opened within minutes of each roster announcement.

Vex's sponsor—a beverage company whose name he could never remember—had given him a list of priorities. Vela's name was fourth on it. The first three were already caught, their amber lights extinguished on his console, their bodies presumably being processed for the triumph ceremonies.

He had a sponsor obligation.

He also had a professional interest. Vela had done something on hour seven that he had never seen a runner do. She had doubled back. Not a feint—a true reversal, through a patch of dead ground where the drones struggled with parallax, into a thicket she must have known contained a real wasps' nest. He had watched, fascinated, as the small shape on his screen disappeared and reappeared, the wasps swirling around her like a cape. The drones had momentarily lost her. When they reacquired, she was half a kilometer southwest, moving in a direction no runner had any tactical reason to move.

*She is not running from me,* Vex had realized, with the small private thrill that was the only honest pleasure his profession afforded him. *She is running from something else. I am merely the second danger.*

This interested him. It also made her more dangerous. People running from specific fears were harder to predict than people running from the generic terror of the hunt.

He waited.

---

Vela heard the wingbeat before she saw the drone.

She knew there were two types. The scout class—small, red-bellied, harmless except as eyes. And the other class, the one the runners called *wraiths*, that would only appear when a hunt was concluding.

This was a scout. It hung in the air perhaps thirty meters up, its lens a black pearl in the grey half-light of the canopy. Vela did not run. Running from a scout was a confession. She walked, with the careful measured gait of someone who had somewhere to be, and tried to think.

The wraith would come for her now. She knew it the way she knew the tracker was warming against her bone. The scout had found her, and somewhere on a console in the world above, a hunter was being told where she was.

She reached the fallen oak. The cache was intact—a metal bottle of water, two ration strips, and a folded piece of paper she had carried for eleven hours without looking at. She had been afraid of the paper. Now she unfolded it, and read it, and folded it again, and put it in her mouth, and chewed until the words were pulp and the taste was iron and salt.

Her name, it had said, in handwriting she had not seen in seven years.

*Vela. If you are reading this, they have caught up with the others. Run south. There is a man with a yellow scarf at the river crossing. He is the only one left.*

She did not know if the man with the yellow scarf was still alive. She did not know if the river crossing was still a crossing, or if the map had lied, or if the paper was itself a trap laid by the Syndicate to test the runners' sentimental attachments.

She ran south.

---

Vex was not a cruel man. This was a fact he liked about himself and which his colleagues found either admirable or suspect. He took no pleasure in the kill. The kill, in his private philosophy, was a kind of punctuation—the period at the end of a long and intricate sentence. What he loved was the sentence itself: the architecture of approach, the slow tightening of the weave, the moment when a runner felt his presence in the forest and began, in some small betraying way, to run differently.

He had begun his approach an hour before the scout had located her. The scout was theater. The hunt was already over.

Vela did not know this. Vela believed, with the religious intensity of the cornered, that she was still being pursued. She ran, and he walked, and the distance between them closed in the slow arithmetic of inevitability.

He watched her through the scope of a rifle that he did not, in this particular moment, intend to fire. The rifle was for emergencies—for the rare runner who turned at bay and fought, who had decided that the humiliation of capture was worse than the brevity of a bullet. Vela was not, he judged, such a runner. Vela was a woman who intended to survive, and who understood, in the marrow of her, that survival sometimes required the act of stopping.

He let her reach the river. He watched her stand at the bank, the grey water moving past her ankles, and he watched her look both ways along the shore for the man with the yellow scarf.

There was no man with a yellow scarf. There had not been one for at least six hours. The Syndicate had found him first.

Vela knew this. Some part of her had always known this. The paper had been a kindness, or a cruelty, and it was difficult, at this late hour, to tell the two apart.

She heard the click of a safety being disengaged, and she did not turn around.

---

There is a particular choreography to a clean claim.

The hunter approaches from the runner's flank—not behind, never directly behind, because the Syndicate's cameras must have their angle. The runner kneels. This is a rule so old it predates the Preserve, predates the Syndicate itself, going back to some forgotten pasture in some forgotten century where one animal would lower its head to another as a kind of grammar.

Vela knelt. The river moved around her knees. The water was cold, colder than it should have been, the climate system running its cooling cycle for the benefit of fish that had been engineered to require it.

Cassian Vex stepped into her field of vision. He was younger than she had expected, and older than he had any right to be. He wore the grey of the registered hunters, and his face had the particular stillness of someone who had learned, long ago, to keep his expressions off his skin.

"Rise," he said, not unkindly. "It's done. You've earned the words."

This was also a rule. A clean claim entitled the runner to a brief statement—a sentence, a paragraph, sometimes, in the case of the very famous or the very eloquent, a small and terrible speech. The Syndicate's audience loved these. They were the soul of the broadcast.

Vela rose. She did not look at the camera drone hovering at a respectful distance. She looked at the river, and at the trees beyond it, and at the sky, which was the color of old pewter.

"Tell my daughter," she said, "that the yellow scarf was real. Tell her I went looking for it."

Then she knelt again, and the river moved on, and the drone recorded, and the world above her turned in its bright and terrible attention to the next amber light on the map.

---

Vex stood for a long time at the bank after the wraith had come and gone. The water had taken Vela's warmth from the stones, and the stones were already giving it back to the air, and the air was giving it to the canopy, and the canopy to the sky.

He was paid per claim. He would be photographed, later, with the runner's effects, the way his sponsors required. The photographs would be transmitted and consumed and argued over, and somewhere in a boardroom a man would commend him, and somewhere in a tavern a stranger would curse him, and these two things would balance out to nothing at all.

He thought of the piece of paper. He had watched Vela unfold it, had not been able to read it, but had observed her face when she did. He wondered what it had said. He wondered who had written it. He wondered, briefly, if the writer was still among the amber lights, or among the extinguished ones, and he understood that the answer did not matter, and that the understanding did not help.

He shouldered his rifle and began walking back toward the extraction point. The forest closed around him. The trees, real and printed, performed their patient pantomime of the wild. Somewhere, a runner he would never meet was still running, and the drones were still watching, and the long bright machinery of the sport turned, and turned, and turned.

# The Weight of the Spade

The whistle screamed, and Private Emil Kael scrambled over the parapet into the sucking mud of No Man's Land. His boots slid, the world reduced to a grey soup of fog and cordite. Somewhere to his left, a flare popped red, and the shadows of men scrambled alongside him. Somewhere ahead, the Germans were doing the same.

Raiding parties, the officers called it. A venture into the dark to take prisoners, to gather intelligence, to remind the enemy we were still here, still human enough to hate them.

The German trench lip loomed out of the murk. Emil dropped into it on top of a body, his hands sinking into a wool greatcoat still warm. Then there was movement in the communication trench—a helmeted shape rising from the shadows, bayonet coming up. Emil swung the trench shovel he'd been given at the depot, a sharpened thing they called a "hod," meant for digging but forged for butchering.

He didn't remember the moment clearly afterward. The flat of the steel connected with the side of the German's head with a sound like a wet mallet striking a melon. The man crumpled. Emil fell on top of him, scrabbling for the shovel, raising it again, bringing it down. Once. Twice. A third time.

The German was young. That was the part Emil couldn't unsee. A soft, dark beard that couldn't have been grown in more than a few weeks. Eyes the color of a spring river that opened wide with surprise, then with something else—recognition, perhaps, that he was nineteen years old and would never go home to the village he had spoken of to his friends in the trench.

Emil hit him again.

---

They did not take prisoners that night. The officer, Lieutenant Mercier, said it had been too confused, too dark. Emil did not contradict him. He walked back to the British line in silence, the shovel still in his hand, its blade dark and heavy. He set it against the trench wall and sat beside it, and for a long time he did not move.

The trench was quiet. The artillery had paused, as it sometimes did, and the only sounds were the distant gurgle of a clogged drain and a horse somewhere behind the line, breathing in the dark.

Emil became aware that his hands were shaking. Then his shoulders. Then some place deep in his chest, a place he had not known existed until that night, a small cold animal that had woken up and would not be put back to sleep. He put his hands on his knees to stop the trembling and felt the wetness there. It was not his own blood.

He had not vomited during the raid. He had not cried. He had not screamed. The thing that had climbed out of him during those seconds in the trench had been something older than any of those, something the recruiting sergeant in Bristol had not thought to mention when he signed the papers. Now it sat in his chest and would not leave.

He thought: *He was a person.*

He had not thought this during the killing. During the killing, the German had been a shape, an obstacle, a thing to be removed so that he himself might remain. The body was a problem to be solved. This was what training did, what the discipline of the line did, what survival required. A man was a target or a threat or a corpse, and the only sane response was the next motion, the next breath, the next step back toward the sound of English voices.

But now, in the silence, the humanity of the dead boy began to reassert itself, and it came back wrong. It came back as a question that had no good answer. The dead boy's mother in some village in Bavaria—what was she doing now? Was she awake, as Emil's mother sometimes was, sitting at the kitchen table with a candle, unable to sleep because she could not stop listening for a footstep on the path?

Emil had killed a man whose mother loved him.

He had done it with a shovel. He had done it three times, because the first two had not seemed enough, because some part of him had been afraid, and fear turned to fury, and fury turned to repetition, and repetition turned into a habit that would sit in his hands for the rest of his life.

A man named Davies came and sat beside him. Davies was from Cardiff, a miner before the war, and he had the patience of a man who had worked underground. He did not ask what had happened. He simply sat.

After a while, he said, "First one?"

Emil nodded.

"It gets easier," Davies said.

It was, Emil would realize many years later, the cruelest thing anyone had ever said to him. Because it was not true. The first one stayed sharp in him. The second, the third, the many that came after—those blurred, ran together like watercolors in the rain. But the first one, the boy with the new beard, stayed clear. He stayed in the trench. He stayed in every quiet room Emil Kael ever sat in for the rest of his life.

The war ended in 1918. Emil Kael lived until 1967. He had a son, who had a son, who has a son of his own now. None of them know the name of the German boy in the trench. Emil never learned it. The records were lost, or never made, and the body was buried in a place that is now a field, with a small wooden cross that rotted decades ago.

But the shovel is in a museum in Belgium. The placard says *British entrenching tool, Western Front, c. 1916.* It does not say what it was used for. It does not say whose blood still clings to it in a thin brown line along the edge of the blade.

Perhaps that is the kindest thing. Perhaps some things should not be said aloud.

Perhaps Emil knew this, when he put the shovel down in the trench that night and sat with his back against the cold wall, listening to the slow breathing of the horse and the slow breathing of the men and the slow breathing of the small cold animal that had taken up residence in his chest.

It would be his companion for forty-nine more years.

He never spoke of it. Not to his wife, not to his son, not to the doctor at the VA who wrote *neurasthenia* on his papers. He carried it the way soldiers carry their wounds—silently, privately, with the strange loyalty one feels toward the thing that has broken one, because at least the breaking is proof that one was there.

He was there. He did what was done. He survived.

The other boy did not.

He was there. He did what was done. He survived.

The other boy did not.

The square smelled of wet stone and yesterday's rain.
